claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Initial Coin Offerings Emerging Practices, Risk Factors, and Red Flags (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3067615
scope_conditions: token offerings based on open source software
claims.supporting_quote: Investors cannot rely on the implicit promise that the token promoters and their developers will increase the value of the acquired token and not create another token with identical features.

claims.claim: Legacy businesses own their code and can sue competitors who copy it, whereas open source crypto start-ups rely only on licenses, and this weaker incentive structure makes ICO investments riskier.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Initial Coin Offerings Emerging Practices, Risk Factors, and Red Flags (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3067615
scope_conditions: open source crypto start-ups compared to legacy code-owning businesses
claims.supporting_quote: While open-source crypto start-ups have licenses that help protect them from competitor companies who may be using their code for profit, legacy businesses that own their code and can sue competitors who copy such code which provides a different incentive structure and makes ICO investments riskier.

claims.claim: On bankruptcy or termination of the platform, token holders typically have no liquidity preference and no recourse at all once debt holders and outside creditors are satisfied, so unlike a venture capital seed investor with at least a simple liquidity preference, they typically lose everything they invested.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Initial Coin Offerings Emerging Practices, Risk Factors, and Red Flags (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3067615
scope_conditions: bankruptcy or termination of the promoter's business or platform
claims.supporting_quote: Again, by contrast, token holders typically lose everything they invested as they have no liquidity preference at all.

claims.claim: The lack of a regulatory framework creates significant legal uncertainty in the ICO market, and because cryptocurrencies are censorship-resistant and arguably regulation-resistant by design, that uncertainty may sooner or later lead the Securities and Exchange Commission to declare ICOs illegal.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Initial Coin Offerings Emerging Practices, Risk Factors, and Red Flags (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3067615
scope_conditions: ICO market as of November 2017
United States securities regulation
claims.supporting_quote: The lack of a regulatory framework creates significant legal uncertainty in the ICO market. Moreover, cryptocurrencies are censorship-resistant and arguably regulation-resistant by design,56

claims.claim: ICOs are not subject to predefined regulatory procedures: whitepapers do not follow prospectus disclosure guidelines, are not reviewed or audited by any authority, and are not subject to any form of rating of the new entrepreneurial initiative.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Initial Coin Offerings Emerging Practices, Risk Factors, and Red Flags (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3067615
scope_conditions: ICO market as of November 2017
claims.supporting_quote: ICOs are not subject to predefined regulatory procedures. Whitepapers do not follow prospectus disclosure guidelines, are not reviewed or unaudited by any authorities and are not subject to any forms of rating of the new entrepreneurial initiatives.

claims.claim: Private initiatives are emerging to fill the ICO disclosure and rating gap, including a joint venture between Ambisafe and the rating agency ICOrating created to ensure high quality standards and support investor due diligence.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Initial Coin Offerings Emerging Practices, Risk Factors, and Red Flags (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3067615
scope_conditions: ICO market as of November 2017
claims.supporting_quote: To combat these shortcomings, a private initiative, a joint-venture between Ambisafe Inc.59 and the Russian-based rating agency ICOrating,60 has been created to ensure high-quality standards, supporting investors in their due-diligence

claims.claim: Identifying legitimate projects and distinguishing them from scams is a necessary condition both for investor protection and for creating the conditions in which ICOs can proliferate.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Initial Coin Offerings Emerging Practices, Risk Factors, and Red Flags (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3067615
scope_conditions: ICO market as of November 2017
claims.supporting_quote: Identifying legitimate projects, distinguishing them from scams, is vital to pursue investors' protection while creating the conditions for ICOs to proliferate.

claims.claim: Zombie ICOs, which have little chance of creating a successful market for their tokens, became increasingly common in 2017 and are identifiable by their inability to answer core questions about the problem solved, the allocation of proceeds, the viability of the product, and the team's business experience.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Initial Coin Offerings Emerging Practices, Risk Factors, and Red Flags (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3067615
scope_conditions: ICO market in 2017
claims.supporting_quote: "Zombie ICOs" are ICOs that really have little chance of creating a successful market for their tokens. Such ICOs have become increasingly common in 2017. Zombie ICOs often cannot succinctly answer core questions in their whitepaper or in response to questions by possible investors.

claims.claim: An ICO that proposes an uncapped raise without an underlying product is a very serious red flag, because uncapped raises are perceived by the crypto community as greedy and raise investor uncertainty about the valuation of the platform or product being bought.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Initial Coin Offerings Emerging Practices, Risk Factors, and Red Flags (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3067615
scope_conditions: ICOs without an underlying product
claims.supporting_quote: First, ICOs that propose uncapped raises without an underlying product constitute a very serious red flag for any investor.

claims.claim: Capped token issuances became the dominant structure between 2016 and 2017 because a cap increases the likelihood that the ICO will be oversubscribed, which creates a significant incentive for investors to attempt to get in first.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Initial Coin Offerings Emerging Practices, Risk Factors, and Red Flags (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3067615
scope_conditions: ICO structures between 2016 and 2017
claims.supporting_quote: Because of such concerns, capped token issuances became the dominant structure between 2016 and 2017. Capped sales increase the likelihood for the ICO promoters that the ICO will be oversubscribed, creating a significant incentive for investors to attempt to get in first.

claims.claim: The Gnosis ICO shows how a reverse dutch auction can mitigate the inefficiencies and risks of a capped sale: the offering was capped at $12.5 million and the time needed to complete the sale determined the quantity of tokens distributed to investors, with the rest held by the start-up team.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Initial Coin Offerings Emerging Practices, Risk Factors, and Red Flags (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3067615
scope_conditions: capped token sales exposed to first mover rush dynamics
claims.supporting_quote: To mitigate the inefficiencies and the risks of a capped sale, the Gnosis ICO was structured as a reverse dutch auction

claims.claim: ICO promoters should not allow tokens to be traded before the underlying protocol network or application is live, and should not use a landing page that focuses almost exclusively on the ICO while providing less content on the product, project, technology, and team.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Initial Coin Offerings Emerging Practices, Risk Factors, and Red Flags (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3067615
scope_conditions: emerging bad ICO practices identified in 2017
claims.supporting_quote: Such practices include allowing tokens to be traded before underlying protocol network or application is live, using a landing page that focuses almost exclusively on the ICO with project timeline etc. but provides less content on product, project, technology, and team.

claims.claim: ICO promoters should make significant and ongoing disclosures on vesting and lockup periods and should never manipulate the smart contract to change ICO sales rules mid-course during the offering.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Initial Coin Offerings Emerging Practices, Risk Factors, and Red Flags (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3067615
scope_conditions: ongoing ICO sales governed by smart contracts
claims.supporting_quote: Moreover, ICO promoters should include significant and ongoing disclosures on vesting and lockup periods, should never manipulate the smart contract to change ICO sales rules mid-course during the ICO.

claims.claim: ICO disclosures should be as clear as possible: promoters should avoid an unclear or uncertain use of proceeds pie chart and should be very clear on plans for converting cryptocurrency into actual company reserves.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Initial Coin Offerings Emerging Practices, Risk Factors, and Red Flags (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3067615
scope_conditions: ICO issuers seeking to meet emerging good practice standards
claims.supporting_quote: Moreover, the ICO disclosures have to be as clear as possible and should avoid an unclear or uncertain use of proceeds pie chart and should be very clear on cryptocurrency conversion plans into actual company reserves.

claims.claim: Through continuous evolution and improvement of ICO practices, the ICO industry and the underlying crypto businesses can become the foundation of the emerging crypto economy.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Initial Coin Offerings Emerging Practices, Risk Factors, and Red Flags (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3067615
scope_conditions: continued voluntary or mandated improvement of ICO industry practice
claims.supporting_quote: Through ICOs' evolution and continuous practice improvements, the ICO industry and underlying crypto businesses can become the foundation of the emerging crypto economy.

claims.claim: The core lawyer characteristics and skillsets produced by the existing legal education and regulatory framework are incompatible with what the practice of law in the 21st century demands.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: existing law school curricula and bar regulatory frameworks
21st century practice conditions shaped by disruptive technology
claims.supporting_quote: Key lawyer characteristics and lawyers' core skillsets in the existing legal education and regulatory framework are incompatible with the demands on lawyers of the 21st century.

claims.claim: Disruptive innovation in law renders obsolete many and probably most of the traditional legal skills and characteristics that law schools currently cultivate.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: areas of practice exposed to disruptive innovation in law
claims.supporting_quote: Yet, disruptive innovation in law9 obviates many if not most of the traditional legal skills and characteristics of traditional lawyers.

claims.claim: Even the law firms that are best at finding innovative solutions for clients remain reluctant to fully adopt Legal Tech innovations, so quality of client service does not predict willingness to adopt.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: law firms and in-house legal departments as of 2017
claims.supporting_quote: While the better firms often find innovative solutions to their clients' problems, even those firms are reluctant to fully embrace Legal Tech innovations.

claims.claim: Law schools that invest early in artificial intelligence, machine learning, and blockchain will gain a comparative advantage over peer schools irrespective of ranking, because demand for lawyers trained in those technologies is likely to spike once law firm adoption crosses a threshold.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: first mover law schools that make the financial investment
a threshold point of law firm adoption is reached
claims.supporting_quote: comparative advantage vis-à-vis their peers, regardless of the ranking of such school, because the demand for lawyers adequately trained in artfical intelligence, machine learning, and blockchain is likely to increase sharply at a threshold point of law firm adoption.

claims.claim: The curriculum of American law schools has changed only marginally over the past thirty plus years, even as the practice environment has been transformed.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: American law schools
period of roughly 1985 to 2017
claims.supporting_quote: The curriculum of American law schools has only marginally changed over the last 30 plus years.

claims.claim: The challenges created by Legal Tech, the new economy, and platform technologies justify a fundamentally more creative and innovative approach to legal education in the 21st century.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
claims.supporting_quote: The challenges presented by Legal Tech, the new economy, and platform technologies justify a more creative and innovative approach for legal education in the 21st century.

claims.claim: The first generations of Legal Tech did not reduce demand for lawyers; by making far greater volumes of legal material available faster, they created a need for additional lawyers to evaluate that material.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: Legal Tech from the 1970s legal databases through early practice management software
claims.supporting_quote: in fact, created the need for additional lawyers to evaluate the new and increasing numbers of legal materials made available faster and more easily accessible by technology.

claims.claim: The decentralization of law pursued by Legal Tech startups has broad repercussions for the legal profession, the first of which is that existing legal services are rendered increasingly irrelevant or are replaced outright by Legal Tech.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: legal services amenable to online delivery, matching, AI review, or blockchain settlement
claims.supporting_quote: The decentralization of law that is a central part of the startup companies' purpose and that disrupts existing legal practices has broad repercussions for the legal profession. First, existing legal services are rendered increasingly irrelevant or are replaced by Legal Tech.

claims.claim: Legal Tech applications will soon perform most of the work junior lawyers do, and will do so without the human elements that produce imprecision, flaws, inaccuracies, potential lawsuits, and delay; junior legal professionals and support staff are therefore the first casualties.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: high volume, standardizable junior lawyer tasks
near future relative to 2017
claims.supporting_quote: Legal Tech applications will be able to perform most of junior lawyers' work in the near future without the human elements that create imprecision, flaws, inaccuracies, possible lawsuits, and delay.

claims.claim: Legal Tech startups will force the legal profession to innovate perpetually, a demand that overextended and cumbersome legal organizations which have lost the capacity for agile reinvention cannot easily meet.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: incumbent legal organizations with traditional hierarchical structures
claims.supporting_quote: the legal profession will be forced by such startup companies to innovate in perpetuity, a task that is not easily accomplished by overextended and — often — cumbersome legal organizations that have lost the capacity for agile re-invention.

claims.claim: Legal Tech's disruptive innovation combined with the principles of the sharing economy requires lawyers and lawmakers to reevaluate their understanding of many areas of law.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: areas of law touched by sharing and decentralized peer to peer platforms
claims.supporting_quote: Legal Tech's disruptive innovation in combination with the principles established by the sharing economy require lawyers and lawmakers to reevaluate their understanding of many areas of the law.

claims.claim: Redesigning legal doctrine around sharing and decentralized peer to peer platforms demands out of the box thinking from a profession whose members were trained, both in law school and across their careers, to think inside the box.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: lawyers trained in conventional law school and practice environments
claims.supporting_quote: Such an undertaking requires out-of-the-box thinking for lawyers who were trained during law school and during their entire careers to think inside the box.

claims.claim: The counseling, deal making, matchmaking, gatekeeping, and enforcement roles historically performed by lawyers are increasingly performed by technology, and blockchain technology and smart contracting will accelerate that substitution.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: transactional legal roles that can be encoded
near future relative to 2017
claims.supporting_quote: However, the counseling, deal-making, matchmaking, gatekeeping, and enforcing roles are increasingly performed by technology.43 This trend is likely to accelerate in the near future, enabled by blockchain technology and smart contracting.

claims.claim: Because a public blockchain is genuinely public and immutable, it increases transparency while simultaneously and significantly reducing transaction costs.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: public blockchains rather than consortium or fully private blockchains
claims.supporting_quote: Because the blockchain (at the least the public blockchain) is in fact public and immutable, the technology increases transparency, while at the same time significantly reducing transaction costs.

claims.claim: Intermediaries, lawyers among them, are replaced by code, connectivity, crowd, and collaboration.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: transactions capable of being executed on blockchain infrastructure
claims.supporting_quote: Intermediaries, including lawyers, are replaced by code, connectivity, crowd, and collaboration.

claims.claim: It is the completely decentralized network connectivity of the blockchain via the Internet, more than the use of digital signatures to establish party identity and authenticity, that provides the strongest protection against fraud.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: fully decentralized, internet connected blockchain networks
claims.supporting_quote: While blockchain's use of digital signatures helps establish the identity and authenticity of the parties involved in the transaction, it is the completely decentralized network connectivity via the Internet that allows the most protection against fraud.

claims.claim: Blockchain's distributed consensus model permits node verification of transactions without compromising the privacy of the parties, which makes it arguably safer than a traditional model requiring third party intermediary validation.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: blockchains using node based distributed consensus
claims.supporting_quote: That model also allows node verification of transactions without compromising the privacy of the parties and is therefore arguably safer than a traditional model that requires third-party intermediary validation of transactions.

claims.claim: Smart contract arrangements involving several parties and greater complexity require the verifiable and unhackable system that blockchain technology supplies.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: multiparty and complex smart contract arrangements
claims.supporting_quote: More complex smart contract arrangements in which several parties are involved require a verifiable and unhackable system provided by blockchain technology.

claims.claim: Smart contracting on a blockchain often makes conventional legal contracting unnecessary, because smart contracts emulate the logic of legal contract clauses.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: transactions whose terms can be expressed in code
claims.supporting_quote: Through blockchain technology, smart contracting often makes contractual legal contracting unnecessary as smart contracts often emulate the logic of legal contract clauses.

claims.claim: Increased connectivity enabled by blockchain technology, combined with increased decentralization, allows the removal of intermediaries including lawyers, financial intermediaries, and platform companies.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: environments where blockchain enabled connectivity and decentralization advance together
claims.supporting_quote: Increased connectivity enabled by blockchain technology in combination with increased decentralization allows for the removal of intermediaries, including lawyers, financial intermediaries, and platform companies.

claims.claim: Venture capital investment in blockchain startups has grown exponentially since 2012, which the authors read as an indicator of the technology's commercial maturity.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: VC investment in blockchain startups, 2007 to 2016
claims.supporting_quote: Figure 2 shows that venture capital (VC) investment in startup companies that utilize blockchain technology has increased exponentially since 2012.

claims.claim: Once blockchain technology gains wider acceptance and its applications reach consumers, existing legal processes and structures will likely be among the first processes to become redundant.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: wider acceptance of blockchain technology
spread of blockchain applications into consumer markets
claims.supporting_quote: When blockchain technology becomes more widely accepted and applications spread into consumer territory, existing legal processes and structures will likely be among the first processes to become redundant.

claims.claim: Leveraging the big data collected through Legal Tech solutions and blockchain applications in combination with machine learning produces more creative and faster tools, which in turn generates a surge of innovative platforms that disrupt the legal industry.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: settings where Legal Tech and blockchain generate usable data at scale
claims.supporting_quote: Leveraging the big data that is collected by using Legal Tech solutions and blockchain applications in combination with machine learning creates more creative and faster tools.

claims.claim: The world of blockchain and smart contracting has clearly not reached maturity, which is the first of several technological and legal limitations facing blockchain and smart contracts.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: state of the technology as of 2017
claims.supporting_quote: First, the world of blockchain and smart contracting has clearly not reached maturity yet.

claims.claim: Contrary to the widespread belief among legal professionals that code can only handle very simple transactions, blockchain enabled smart contracts generally do not require legal involvement across the spectrum of transactions.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: transactions capable of being coded
contested against the prevailing view in the legal community
claims.supporting_quote: While blockchain-enabled smart contracts generally do not require legal involvement across the spectrum of transactions, legal professionals often still believe that "code" in smart contracts can only deal with very simple transactions

claims.claim: Because the legal origin of smart contracting is unsettled, lawyers may argue that smart contracts are void and unenforceable under the law even where the smart contract accurately reflects the parties' underlying agreement.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: smart contracts assessed under existing contract law doctrine
claims.supporting_quote: While smart contracts may reflect the underlying contract between parties, lawyers may argue that "smart contracts" are void and unenforceable under the law.

claims.claim: Contract law rules on formation, interpretation, conditions, and remedies require substantive adjustment before smart contracts can be accommodated.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: existing contract law doctrine applied to blockchain smart contracts
claims.supporting_quote: Contractual legal rules regarding formation, interpretation, conditions, and remedies require substantive adjustments of smart contracts in contract law.

claims.claim: Although blockchain technology itself offers unprecedented data and privacy protection, storing blockchain data across a global network of nodes often will not comply with the consumer protection rules, directives, and guidelines of particular jurisdictions.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: global node distribution of blockchain data
jurisdiction specific consumer protection and data rules
claims.supporting_quote: While blockchain technology itself offers unprecedented genuine data and privacy protection, the storage of blockchain data across a global network of nodes often will not comply with specific consumer protection rules, directives, and guidelines around the world.

claims.claim: The legal disputes already generated by sharing platforms indicate that future blockchain enabled sharing services will not be accepted quickly or without resistance from incumbents whose service or product delivery is challenged.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: blockchain enabled sharing services entering markets with entrenched incumbents
claims.supporting_quote: The existing legal issues arising in the context of sharing platforms,83 demonstrate that future blockchain- enabled sharing services may not be accepted quickly and without resistance on the part of incumbents challenged by new ways of delivering a service or product.

claims.claim: Fundamental flaws in the DAO's code let hackers move one third of its total funds to a subsidiary account, and that hack together with further technological limitations destroyed the DAO initiative.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: the DAO as launched in May 2016 on Ethereum
claims.supporting_quote: Alas, things went terribly wrong with the DAO. Fundamental flaws in the DAO code enabled hackers to transfer one-third of the total funds to a subsidiary account.92 This hack in combination with additional technological limitations brought down the DAO initiative.

claims.claim: Because a series of smart contracts granted DAO token holders voting rights, the blockchain based smart contracts performed the function of articles of association or corporate bylaws, in an organization that had no directors, managers, or employees.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: decentralized autonomous organizations structured like the DAO
claims.supporting_quote: Because a series of smart contracts granted DAO token holders voting rights, the blockchain-based smart contracts imitated the role of articles of association or bylaws.

claims.claim: Open legal questions about the DAO, including which regime governs token issuance, minority token holder protection, taxation, the binding force of DAO smart contracts, ownership of intellectual property, and conflict resolution, must be answered before future DAO structures can operate seamlessly.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: future decentralized autonomous organization setups
claims.supporting_quote: Open legal issues pertaining to the DAO need to be addressed before future DAO setups can operate seamlessly.

claims.claim: Exponentially increasing disruptive innovation will lead clients to routinely bring legal professionals problems that those lawyers cannot fully understand, inside a legal framework that does not always supply clear or helpful answers.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: worldwide acceleration of disruptive innovation
claims.supporting_quote: The exponentially increasing disruptive innovation worldwide will cause clients to frequently ask legal professionals to deal with issues lawyers cannot fully understand, within a legal framework that does not always offer clear or helpful answers.

claims.claim: Law schools should educate lawyers who add value by helping clients and society adjust to the technological environment rather than lawyers who impose unnecessary or unwise restrictions on it, since such restrictions will not stop technological development anyway.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
claims.supporting_quote: Law schools need to find ways to educate lawyers who can add value in helping clients and society adjust to our increasing technological environment rather than who will create unnecessary or unwise restrictions on it.

claims.claim: The traditional legal tool kit worked adequately when innovation cycles were long, but where innovation is exponential it is regularly out of touch with the radically different needs of a decentralized world and often produces disastrous outcomes.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: exponential rather than long innovation cycles
decentralized technological environments
claims.supporting_quote: This approach might have worked adequately when innovation cycles were longer, but in a world where innovations occur exponentially, the traditional legal tool kit is regularly out of touch with the radically different needs of a decentralized world.

claims.claim: Most lawyers and law industry representatives underestimate the implications of emerging Legal Tech.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: law firm and corporate lawyers in Asia, Europe, and the United States
claims.supporting_quote: Most lawyers and law industry representatives underestimate the implications of the emerging Legal Tech.

claims.claim: Advising on blockchain contracts requires that law students and lawyers become familiar with the technology and learn at least basic coding as it pertains to Ethereum smart contracts.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: lawyers who intend to advise on blockchain based contracts
claims.supporting_quote: In order to advise on blockchain contracts, law students and lawyers have to become familiar with the technology and learn at least basic coding as it pertains to Ethereum smart contracts.

claims.claim: Law schools must enable students to work in interdisciplinary teams with software engineers, and a greater appreciation of how code can be used and integrated in legal contexts is essential to that capability.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: law school curricular design for 21st century practice
claims.supporting_quote: law schools need to enable their students to work in interdisciplinary teams with software engineers. A greater appreciation of the means by which code can be utilized and integrated in legal contexts is essential.

claims.claim: Future lawyers will have to distinguish blockchain based contracting from traditional legal contracting and advise clients on the optimal allocation between the two.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: dealmaking that mixes blockchainable and non blockchainable elements
claims.supporting_quote: For instance, future lawyers will have to be able to distinguish blockchain-based contracting from traditional legal contracting and advise clients on optimal blockchain and non-blockchain contracting allocations.

claims.claim: For the parts of dealmaking and other legal tasks that cannot be placed on a blockchain, the role of non blockchainable agents of trust may expand, and blockchain driven disintermediation of law may itself create additional legal tasks requiring human lawyers.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: legal tasks that require the ambiguity and flexibility of law
claims.supporting_quote: For the parts of dealmaking and the other legal tasks that are non-blockchainable, the role for other, non-blockchainable agents of trust may expand. It seems possible that the blockchain-driven disintermediation of law itself creates additional legal tasks that require human lawyer input.

claims.claim: The Investment Advisers Act safe harbor let an adviser count an entire legal organization as one client, provided the advice followed the organization's objectives rather than those of its individual owners, which is what allowed advisers to manage money for hundreds of underlying investors while staying exempt.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Investment Fund Regulation - Theory and Empirical Evidence from 1998 to 2016 (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2998097
scope_conditions: United States
before the Dodd-Frank Act of 2010
claims.supporting_quote: investment advisers to private investment funds were able to count a legal organization as a single client provided the investment advice was based on the objectives of the legal organization rather than the individual investment objectives of any owners of the legal organization.

claims.claim: The 2004 registration rule failed in court because the term client was not defined in the Investment Advisers Act, leaving the SEC without authority to fix its meaning, and the D.C. Circuit vacated the rule in Goldstein as arbitrary rulemaking.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Investment Fund Regulation - Theory and Empirical Evidence from 1998 to 2016 (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2998097
scope_conditions: United States
Goldstein v. SEC, July 2006
claims.supporting_quote: Because the term "client" had not otherwise been defined in the Investment Advisers Act, the SEC had no authority to determine the meaning of the term.

claims.claim: Because banks and brokers had let LTCM borrow the full value of its collateral, LTCM's 4.8 billion dollars in capital dissipated quickly once banks began making margin calls.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Investment Fund Regulation - Theory and Empirical Evidence from 1998 to 2016 (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2998097
scope_conditions: LTCM, 1998
100 percent collateral lending by banks and brokers
claims.supporting_quote: Because banks and brokers had allowed LTCM to borrow 100 percent of the value of its collateral prior to the worsening of LTCM's financial condition in 1998, LTCM's $4.8 billion in capital dissipated quickly when the banks began to make margin calls.

claims.claim: Banks overexposed themselves to private investment fund lending, which allowed LTCM and similar funds to grow significantly and led banks as counterparties to put their own existence at risk.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Investment Fund Regulation - Theory and Empirical Evidence from 1998 to 2016 (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2998097
scope_conditions: banks lending to private investment funds
pre 1998 lending practices
claims.supporting_quote: However, banks overexposed themselves to private investment fund lending, allowing LTCM and other private investment funds to grow significantly. As counterparties to private investment funds, such as LTCM, banks put their own existence at risk with their lending practices.

claims.claim: Post LTCM proposals for clearer credit risk strategies and credit risk management policies at financial intermediaries were inappropriately applied across the whole range of business models and lacked concrete implementation elements.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Investment Fund Regulation - Theory and Empirical Evidence from 1998 to 2016 (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2998097
scope_conditions: post LTCM regulatory proposals
author's critique beginning in 2005
claims.supporting_quote: He found that proposals involving clearer credit risk strategies and credit risk management policies and processes for financial intermediaries were inappropriately applied across the range of business models and lacked concrete implementation elements.

claims.claim: Stress tests, Value at Risk, and Monte Carlo scenarios imposed on financial intermediaries that lend to private investment funds necessarily rely on historical data, so they are of limited value as indicators of high risk sensitivity to future events.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Investment Fund Regulation - Theory and Empirical Evidence from 1998 to 2016 (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2998097
scope_conditions: risk models used by intermediaries exposed to private funds

claims.claim: The obstacles preventing consumers and entrepreneurs from accessing a workable new technology are frequently not technological limits but human choices embodied in law: legal and regulatory rules prohibit or limit commercial exploitation of, and public access to, new technology.

scope_conditions: under the legal frameworks in force as of 2017
claims.supporting_quote: Because national and international law do not currently recognize AI as a subject of law, AI has no legal personality and as such cannot be held personally liable for damages.

claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: where big data is used as a basis for analysis or inference
claims.supporting_quote: Foundational data issues of construct validity, measurement, reliability, and data dependencies are the same regardless of data quantities.

claims.claim: Regulation is never grounded in the full set of facts about a technology; it is always premised on a prior selection of the facts that regulators themselves treat as relevant when deciding what, when, and how to intervene.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
claims.supporting_quote: In this respect, regulation is always premised on a selection of relevant facts about a particular technology.

technologies developing at exponential rates
claims.supporting_quote: The time frame for rulemaking in the existing regulatory infrastructure is largely inadequate to address regulatory challenges associated with disruptive innovation.

claims.supporting_quote: The speed of product innovation makes it possible to bring a new product to market while formal rulemaking in the existing regulatory infrastructure, taking months and often years of regulatory procedure, is still dealing with the last product launch.

scope_conditions: rules aimed at products subject to rapid innovation cycles
claims.supporting_quote: New regulations pertaining to an innovative product could be obsolete before they are finalized.

claims.supporting_quote: The existing regulatory infrastructure cannot sufficiently distinguish and harness beneficial innovation.

claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531

existing rulemaking framework
claims.supporting_quote: technological transition is going to be a permanent state in the age of disruptive innovation, rulemakers' inability to address regulatory issues associated with disruptive innovation will likely generate high levels of legal uncertainty and inconsistency

claims.supporting_quote: The current regulatory framework lacks a mechanism that succinctly and anticipatorily informs rulemakers of beneficial innovative ideas.

claims.claim: Establishing the facts about a new technology is often impossible in practice because there is no adequate sample or other reliable data on the effects of that technology yet.

claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531

claims.supporting_quote: In this respect, the "relevant facts" that form the basis of regulation are never going to be obvious or settled. The regulation of any disruptive new technology is always going to be reactive and based on an uncertain and politicized factual basis.

claims.supporting_quote: Too often, regulators define "success" in negative terms, as in the avoidance of catastrophe.

claims.claim: Because regulators seek to avoid grounds for criticism, they inevitably adopt an overly cautious posture, which is what the precautionary principle amounts to in practice.

claims.supporting_quote: Avoiding grounds for criticism inevitably results in an overly cautious approach, called the "precautionary principle."

claims.claim: Regulatory caution produces a systematic disconnect between the regulation of an innovation and the commercial and consumer ability to access it.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531

claims.supporting_quote: The result is that, all too often, there is a disconnect between regulation and commercial and consumer access to that innovation.

claims.claim: Faced with disruptive innovation, regulators believe their only options are reckless action, meaning regulation without sufficient facts, or paralysis, meaning doing nothing; in that bind caution beats risk and the precautionary principle becomes the default.

Inevitably in such a case, caution tends to trump risk. The precautionary principle becomes the default position.

claims.claim: Regulatory caution is not neutral: it functions to reinforce the status quo, with the result that new technologies struggle to reach the market in a timely or efficient manner.

claims.supporting_quote: But such caution merely functions to reinforce the status quo and the result is that new technologies struggle to reach the market in a timely or efficient manner.

claims.claim: A fact based approach to regulation worked relatively well only under a specific historical condition: innovation cycles were long and disruption unfolded over decades, giving regulators time to get their facts in order before intervening.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: past eras of slow technological disruption
claims.supporting_quote: In spite of these problems, a fact–based approach to regulation may have worked relatively well in the past when innovation cycles were longer and the pace of disruptive innovation occurred over decades.

claims.claim: The automobile illustrates how long the old disruption lag was: Benz's engine did not displace the horse and carriage industry, and mainstream adoption came only in 1908 when Ford began mass producing the Model T, decades after the 1879 patent.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: the origins of the modern automobile industry
claims.supporting_quote: However, Benz's engine did not disrupt the horse and carriage industry or bring the automobile into the mainstream of everyday life. This only occurred much later, in 1908, when Henry Ford started to mass produce the Model T.

claims.claim: The delegation of technology policy to politicians advised by experts rested on public trust that has since eroded: consistent empirical evidence shows that trust in both government and experts has declined in recent years.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: recent decades, drawing on Pew survey evidence
claims.supporting_quote: Although the public once had a relatively high degree of trust in both the political process and the scientific/expert method, consistent empirical evidence demonstrates that both trust in government and experts has declined in recent years.

claims.claim: Time pressure produces two distinct fact failures: the facts about a new technology may simply not exist yet, or regulators may select the wrong, contested, or irrelevant facts as the basis of regulation.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: conditions of incessant and accelerating technological change
claims.supporting_quote: The pressure of time means that the facts surrounding a piece of new technology or other innovation may not be there, or the regulators may simply select the "wrong" — or at least contested or otherwise irrelevant — facts as the basis of regulation.

claims.claim: In the Airbnb case, the selection of the relevant facts and the residency rule that followed from it benefit vested interests, most obviously the hotel industry that stands to lose from Airbnb's competition.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: short term rental rules requiring hosts to reside in the property
claims.supporting_quote: Of course, the selection of the "relevant facts" in this case and the resulting rule benefits certain vested interests, most obviously the hotel industry who stand to lose out from the new competition from Airbnb.

claims.claim: The premises on which regulation of a new technology is built may not be facts at all, or at least not the most relevant facts about that innovation, as the assumption that Airbnb hosts are simply chasing easy money illustrates.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: regulation of platform based innovations such as Airbnb
claims.supporting_quote: The selected facts may not even be facts, or at least, the most relevant facts about a particular innovation.

claims.claim: Contesting the safety rationale offered for restricting Uber, the authors argue that the two way rating system and the algorithmic matching of drivers and customers already provide an effective means of policing drivers and ensuring a safe ride.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: ride hailing platforms with reciprocal ratings and algorithmic matching
claims.supporting_quote: The two–way rating system (drivers rate customers and customers rate drivers) and an algorithm–based system for matching up drivers and customers appear to offer an effective means of policing Uber drivers and ensuring a safe ride for customers.

claims.claim: There is a systematic disconnect between the facts regulators identify as important and the actual experience and wishes of most consumers.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: regulatory debates over platform services such as Uber
claims.supporting_quote: There is a disconnect between the facts that regulators identify as important and the experience and wishes of most consumers.

claims.claim: The problem is not regulator bad faith: the acceleration of innovation cycles means that selecting the relevant facts is difficult even under the best conditions and with the best intentions, while simply waiting is likely to bring further complications and criticism.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: accelerating innovation cycles
independent of agency capture
claims.supporting_quote: the acceleration in innovation cycles means that even in the best conditions and with the best of intentions, selecting relevant facts is a difficult task. And the option of simply waiting seems likely to result in further complications and criticism.

claims.claim: The post truth diagnosis is self defeating as a basis for regulation: if there is no objective basis on which to act, the conclusion is inertia or reproduction of the status quo, which is precisely the regulatory paralysis the diagnosis purports to describe.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: if the skeptical post fact account of regulation is accepted
claims.supporting_quote: If we live in a post–truth world then we don't have any objective basis on which to act, leading to inertia or the reproduction of the status quo.

claims.claim: The response to contested facts should not be to abandon facts, but to identify alternative grounds for regulation that would make the regulation of innovative products and services more effective and more legitimate.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
claims.supporting_quote: And yet, rather than abandoning facts, we should be thinking about some alternative grounds for regulation that would allow the regulation of innovative products and services to be more effective and legitimate.

claims.claim: In a world where regulatory competition is the new normal, regulators can pay a heavy economic price for being overly cautious or for abandoning the attempt to establish a meaningful basis for regulation, because first mover markets capture the benefits.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: global markets with mobile investment and jurisdictional competition
claims.supporting_quote: regulators can pay a heavy economic price for being overly cautious or abandoning the project of trying to establish a meaningful basis for regulation.

claims.claim: Lawmaking and regulatory design need to become more proactive, dynamic, and responsive.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
claims.supporting_quote: Lawmaking and regulatory design needs to become more proactive, dynamic and responsive.

claims.claim: Data on investment in new technology can be used as an index or proxy for the necessity of regulation, supplying the signal that fact based regulation cannot generate in time.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: where venture and investment data on the technology are available
claims.supporting_quote: Of particular importance in this context, is data relating to investment in new technology and innovation.90 Such data can be used as an index or proxy of the necessity of regulation.

claims.claim: Using investment data would let regulators act proactively, avoid wasting resources on technologies unlikely to reach the market, and define the scope of a technology more accurately by focusing on the type of firm attracting investor attention.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
claims.supporting_quote: This might then allow regulators to be more pro–active and avoid wasting resources on technologies that are unlikely to make it to market. It would also allow regulators to more accurately define the scope of a technology by focusing on the type of firm that is attracting attention.

claims.claim: Data on the timing of investment is a reliable indicator of a technology's commercial maturity, because high levels of investor activity signal that the technology is about to be ready for commercial exploitation, which tells regulators when to intervene.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: when early stage investments peak and later stage investments take off
claims.supporting_quote: Data on the timing of investment appears to provide a reliable indicator of the commercial maturity of a technology, in the sense that high levels of investor activity indicate that a particular technology is about to be ready for commercial exploitation.

claims.claim: Regulation should be demand driven, meaning its substantive direction should follow the interests of consumers, and where there is genuine demand for a product or technology it should in principle be permitted.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: where genuine consumer demand for the technology can be shown
claims.supporting_quote: If there is a genuine demand for certain products or technologies, then such technologies should, in principle, be permitted.

claims.claim: A demand driven approach does not require ignoring the risks and negative side effects of new technology; what it requires is that entrenched interests with a clear stake in obstructing a disruptive product or service not be allowed to dominate the debate.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
claims.supporting_quote: What it does mean, however, is that entrenched interests with a clear interest in obstructing a disruptive product or service should not be allowed to dominate the debate.

claims.claim: Regulatory experimentation matters within a single jurisdiction and not only across jurisdictions, because it gives regulators data on the real world effects of a particular regulatory scheme in a comparable setting.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: comparable settings within one jurisdiction
claims.supporting_quote: But such experimentation is also important within a particular jurisdiction as it provides regulators with data on the real–world effects of a particular regulatory scheme in a comparable setting.

claims.claim: Regulators must abandon their fixation on finality and legal certainty and instead treat regulatory decisions as contingent and open ended stages in a longer process.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: regulation of fast moving technologies
claims.supporting_quote: Regulators need to abandon a fixation on finality and legal certainty and embrace contingency, flexibility and an openness to new ideas.

claims.claim: A principle based approach gives regulators greater openness and flexibility and prevents innovative technologies and the companies developing them from becoming bogged down in the regulatory thicket produced by a rule focused approach.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: regulation of disruptive technologies
claims.supporting_quote: a principle–based approach facilitates a greater degree of openness and flexibility on the part of regulators, and prevents innovative technologies (and the companies that have developed them) from becoming bogged down in the regulatory thicket that often results from a rule–focused approach.

claims.claim: The principle based approach has a shortcoming the authors concede: it is usually impossible to comply with principles that could change after the fact, and the approach may let regulators promulgate fact based laws and rules through the backdoor.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: from the perspective of regulated companies operating under principles
claims.supporting_quote: The argument is that it is usually impossible to comply with principles that could change "after the fact."107 That is to say, a principle–based approach may facilitate policy makers, lawmakers, and regulators in promulgating facts–based laws and rules through the backdoor.

claims.claim: The regulatory sandbox provides a safe space in which innovative products and services can be tested without being forced to comply with the otherwise applicable set of rules and regulations.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: the FCA sandbox announced in April 2016 for Fintech firms
claims.supporting_quote: The idea behind the sandbox is to provide a safe space for testing innovative products and services without being forced to comply with the applicable set of rules and regulations.

claims.claim: The most interesting feature of the sandbox is that ideas, products, and services are tested in a live environment, made possible by a set of default parameters the FCA defined that can be altered case by case.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: default duration of three to six months
customer numbers sufficient for statistically relevant data
pre agreed safeguards and disclosure to customers
claims.supporting_quote: What is perhaps most interesting about the sandbox is that new ideas, product, and services can be tested in a "live" environment.112 In order to create this environment, the FCA defined a set of default parameters that can be altered on a case–by–case basis.

claims.claim: The sandbox generates legitimacy as well as information: because the tested technology remains open to discussion and democratic supervision, public entitlement to participate in regulatory debates creates a renewed sense of legitimacy that justifies the regulation.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: where the technology has consequences that flow into everyday lives
claims.supporting_quote: In this way, public entitlement to participate in regulatory debates can help to create a renewed sense of legitimacy that justifies the regulation.

claims.claim: A data based regulatory environment requires measures built on flexible and inclusive processes that involve startups and established companies, regulators, experts, and the public.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: data based regulatory environments
claims.supporting_quote: In a data–based regulatory environment there is a clear need for measures that are built on flexible and inclusive processes that involve startups and established companies, regulators, experts and the public.

claims.claim: The flexible, data based, sandbox style regulatory approach already adopted in the financial industry is expected to expand into other areas of innovation and technology.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: starting from financial regulation
claims.supporting_quote: This regulatory approach is already adopted in the financial industry. It is only to be expected that this trend will expand to other areas

claims.claim: The 1991 passage of Section 7.32 of the Model Business Corporation Act triggered a wave of state authorization of shareholder control agreements, adopted specifically to secure the validity of such agreements rather than leaving validity to uncertain judicial development.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Shareholder Agreements - National Report of the United States of America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3017612
scope_conditions: United States state corporate law
post 1991
claims.supporting_quote: Since Section 7.32 of the Model Business Corporation Act (MBCA) was passed in 1991, most US states have authorized shareholder control agreements in an effort to support the validity of such agreements.

claims.claim: US corporate codes function as enabling statutes that give enterprises wide flexibility, but that flexibility stops at mandatory provisions, which the parties cannot contract around.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Shareholder Agreements - National Report of the United States of America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3017612
scope_conditions: United States corporate codes
claims.supporting_quote: While corporate codes are viewed as "enabling" statutes—providing flexibility for different enterprises—mandatory provisions cannot be changed.

claims.claim: Although shareholder agreements are authorized and shaped by corporation code provisions, their construction is governed by ordinary contract interpretation rules, so statutory authorization does not displace contract doctrine.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Shareholder Agreements - National Report of the United States of America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3017612
scope_conditions: United States, Delaware law illustrated by Salamone v. Gorman
claims.supporting_quote: While the agreements are governed by legislation, general rules applicable to contract interpretation govern the construction of shareholder agreements.

claims.claim: Shareholder agreement terms that limit board authority are vulnerable to invalidation, and the dominant judicial rationale is that such agreements tie the hands of directors and make it impossible for them to exercise discretion over the matters the agreement settles.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Shareholder Agreements - National Report of the United States of America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3017612
scope_conditions: provisions that encroach on the directors' statutory authority to manage the business and affairs of the corporation
claims.supporting_quote: Courts offer varying rationales for nullifying terms of shareholder agreements that limit the board's authority, but most often, courts worry the agreements "tie the hands of the directors," making it impossible for them to exercise their discretion concerning matters decided in the agreement.

claims.claim: Under MBCA Section 7.32 the ten year duration limit is only a default rule, unlike the corresponding limit for voting trusts, so parties who specify a longer term are permitted to have it.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Shareholder Agreements - National Report of the United States of America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3017612
scope_conditions: agreements formed under MBCA Section 7.32
claims.supporting_quote: The section specifies a 10 year limit, a similar period to voting trusts, but unlike voting trusts, this period is just a default rule, so that if the parties specify a longer period it is permitted.

claims.claim: Duration ceilings contained in voting trust statutes do not carry over to other types of shareholder agreements, and courts have repeatedly sustained shareholder agreements intended to run indefinitely.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Shareholder Agreements - National Report of the United States of America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3017612
scope_conditions: agreements other than voting trusts
claims.supporting_quote: Duration limitations in the voting trust statutes do not apply to other types of shareholders' agreements.15 Numerous decisions have sustained shareholders' agreements which were to remain in effect indefinitely.

claims.claim: Because public and close corporation shareholders differ materially in bargaining power, close corporation shareholders should be granted greater flexibility to order their affairs by agreement.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Shareholder Agreements - National Report of the United States of America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3017612
scope_conditions: closely held corporations
claims.supporting_quote: Courts and academics have acknowledged there is a significant difference between shareholders of public and close corporations, specifically in regards to bargaining power, such that close corporation shareholders should have greater flexibility to align their affairs as they see fit.

claims.claim: A shareholder agreement authorized under MBCA Section 7.32 ceases to be effective once the corporation's stock is listed on a national securities exchange or regularly traded in a dealer maintained market, so the going public event terminates the arrangement.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Shareholder Agreements - National Report of the United States of America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3017612
scope_conditions: MBCA jurisdictions
corporation becomes publicly traded
claims.supporting_quote: agreement ceases to be effective when the stock of the corporation is listed on a national securities exchange or regularly traded in a market maintained by one or more members of a national or affiliated securities association.

claims.claim: MBCA Section 7.32 requires unanimity, so agreements that bind only a block of shareholders rather than all of them cannot rely on that section and must find authorization elsewhere.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Shareholder Agreements - National Report of the United States of America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3017612
scope_conditions: agreements seeking MBCA Section 7.32 protection
claims.supporting_quote: Most importantly the agreement must be unanimous, so that agreements that do not involve all shareholders, such as agreements designed to keep control within a block, must look elsewhere for their authorization.

claims.claim: MBCA Section 7.32 requires a writing but, departing from earlier statutes, does not require the agreement to sit in the articles or bylaws, so stand alone written shareholder agreements are expressly valid.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Shareholder Agreements - National Report of the United States of America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3017612
scope_conditions: MBCA Section 7.32 agreements
claims.supporting_quote: The agreement must be in writing, but unlike some earlier statutes, the written agreement does not have to be in the articles or bylaws—stand-alone written agreements are specifically allowed.

claims.claim: The Model Act conditions the arrangement on notice to the market for shares by requiring a legend on the stock certificates that flags the agreement to purchasers of covered shares.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Shareholder Agreements - National Report of the United States of America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3017612
scope_conditions: MBCA Section 7.32 agreements
claims.supporting_quote: Finally, the Model Act language requires that a legend appear on the stock certificates flagging the agreement for purchasers who buy shares covered by such an agreement.

claims.claim: Shareholder agreements matter more in closely held corporations because minority holders have sunk substantial time or capital into the enterprise yet cannot exit through sale, since their shares lack a ready market.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Shareholder Agreements - National Report of the United States of America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3017612
scope_conditions: closely held corporations
dissatisfied minority shareholders
claims.supporting_quote: Minority shareholders in a closely held corporation are likely to have invested substantial time or capital in the enterprise, but those dissatisfied with the corporation's operation cannot sell their shares easily because the shares are not readily marketable.

claims.claim: Voting arrangements are not self executing: their existence does not relieve the corporation of observing the legal formalities of director and shareholder action.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Shareholder Agreements - National Report of the United States of America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3017612
scope_conditions: voting trusts, pooling agreements, and irrevocable proxies
claims.supporting_quote: Voting arrangements are not self-executing, and the mere existence of a voting arrangement does not mean that the corporation should dispense with the legal formalities of director and shareholder actions.

claims.claim: Courts are split on whether a corporation is bound by a shareholder agreement it did not sign: some hold the corporation bound where all shareholders are parties to a valid agreement, while others refuse to bind it.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Shareholder Agreements - National Report of the United States of America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3017612
scope_conditions: all shareholders are parties to the agreement
corporation is not formally a party
claims.supporting_quote: Additionally, if all shareholders of a corporation are parties to a valid agreement, courts have held the corporation bound by the agreement even if it is not formally a party to it.46 Other courts have not found the corporation to be bound.

claims.claim: Corporate claims frequently go unpursued because the decision to sue rests with directors who are often the wrongdoers themselves, which is why shareholders resort to derivative actions.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Shareholder Agreements - National Report of the United States of America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3017612
scope_conditions: injury is to the corporation rather than to shareholders individually
claims.supporting_quote: When the corporation is harmed, it is the corporation that has the claim, but directors are often unwilling to pursue claims, especially when they are the wrongdoers.

claims.claim: A shareholder suing derivatively sues on the corporation's behalf and cannot convert the action into a personal one, even where the corporate injury has impaired the value of that shareholder's own stock.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Shareholder Agreements - National Report of the United States of America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3017612
scope_conditions: injury runs to the corporation
claims.supporting_quote: The shareholders are simply suing on the corporation's behalf and cannot maintain actions on their own behalf to redress an injury to the corporation even if the value of their stock is impaired as a result of the injury.

claims.claim: To escape the procedural hurdles of derivative litigation and recover directly, a shareholder must persuade the court that those abusing control of the corporation harmed the shareholder directly rather than the entity.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Shareholder Agreements - National Report of the United States of America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3017612
scope_conditions: direct as opposed to derivative suits
Delaware courts ask who suffered the harm and who would receive the recovery
claims.supporting_quote: To avoid some of the procedural hurdles of derivative litigation and enable direct recovery, shareholders must convince the court that individuals abusing control of the corporation were directly harming the shareholders.

claims.claim: Under the MBCA a purchaser of shares who bought without knowledge of an existing shareholder control agreement may obtain rescission of the purchase.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Shareholder Agreements - National Report of the United States of America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3017612
scope_conditions: purchaser lacked knowledge of the agreement at the time of purchase
claims.supporting_quote: Under the MBCA, rescission may also be available to a purchaser of shares who did not have knowledge of the existence of a shareholder control agreement at the time of purchase.

claims.claim: Veto rights are the price minority shareholders extract for capital: minority holders may withhold capital contributions unless they receive veto powers over major corporate decisions.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Shareholder Agreements - National Report of the United States of America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3017612
scope_conditions: closely held corporations seeking minority capital
claims.supporting_quote: For example, minority shareholders may refuse to provide capital contributions unless they are granted veto powers over major corporate decisions such as asset sales,
