claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Blockchain-Based Securities Offerings (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3411110
scope_conditions: Overstock Series A digital securities traded on the PRO ATS
claims.supporting_quote: The core difference between the OSTK offering and a traditional securities offering is that the purchaser of OSTK must hold the record directly and as beneficial owner of the securities could not delegate the authority to hold the securities to the broker

claims.claim: Because direct ownership on a blockchain removes the need for the Depository Trust Corporation to hold the certificate and for a broker to record beneficial ownership, agency costs can be cut and ownership clarity increases.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Blockchain-Based Securities Offerings (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3411110
scope_conditions: direct registration of ownership on the ledger
no third party custodian
claims.supporting_quote: By establishing a system that makes the DTC obsolete, agency costs have the potential to be cut and clarity surrounding ownership will increase.

claims.claim: The compliance burden attached to operating an alternative trading system, including fees, consumer protection, examination, and books and records requirements, is typically cost prohibitive for startups.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Blockchain-Based Securities Offerings (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3411110
scope_conditions: startup firms seeking to operate an ATS
SEC and FINRA compliance regime
claims.supporting_quote: ATS compliance costs are typically cost prohibitive for startups.

claims.claim: Running an alternative trading system on a blockchain cures the ATS system's traditional price discovery latency, because every trade is posted to a public ledger that everyone can access.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Blockchain-Based Securities Offerings (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3411110
scope_conditions: ATS operating on a public blockchain ledger
claims.supporting_quote: By creating an ATS that trades securities over blockchain, there is no latency in price discovery, which has traditionally been a criticism of the ATS system. This is because every trade is posted to a public ledger to which everyone has access.

claims.claim: Naked or out of the box short selling is possible only because settlement takes three days, so eliminating the window between trade and settlement on a blockchain eliminates that abuse.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Blockchain-Based Securities Offerings (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3411110
scope_conditions: multi-day settlement regimes such as T+3
claims.supporting_quote: This tactic is only possible because it takes three days to settle a trade. By eliminating the window between trade and settlement, the blockchain eliminates out-of- the-box shorting.

claims.claim: Blockchain removes the class of costs generated by human error in record keeping, because it eliminates the possibility that transactions are misreported in ways that cause irreparable harm.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Blockchain-Based Securities Offerings (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3411110
scope_conditions: record keeping for securities issuance and transfer
claims.supporting_quote: Blockchain technology allows corporations to eliminate costs associated with human errors in record keeping. Blockchain eliminates the possibility of transactions being misreported due to human error that can cause irreparable harm.

claims.claim: Transfer agents become unnecessary in blockchain based trading models because every function they perform, including maintaining the holding record, can be automated in code and is already produced by the ledger's design.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Blockchain-Based Securities Offerings (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3411110
scope_conditions: fully blockchain based trading and settlement models
claims.supporting_quote: In blockchain- based trading models, transfer agents will not be needed because every task they preform can be automated through coding.

claims.claim: The double spending problem has not been eradicated in theory: a group or syndicate obtaining 51 percent control of a network could reverse transactions and create a private chain that the market could only limitedly discern as not real.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Blockchain-Based Securities Offerings (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3411110
scope_conditions: a decentralized network where one party can amass majority hashing control
claims.supporting_quote: There is the possibility a group or syndicate could gain 51% control over the network and would therefore be able to reverse transactions and create a private blockchain, which the market could only limitedly discern as not real.

claims.claim: Any settlement completed in less than ten seconds removes counterparty risk and with it systemic risk entirely, which makes settlement speed, not disclosure, the operative variable for systemic risk.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Blockchain-Based Securities Offerings (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3411110
scope_conditions: settlement finality achieved in under ten seconds
if such speed is ever achieved in any setting
claims.supporting_quote: Most importantly, any settlement that takes less than 10 seconds, if ever achieved in any setting, removes counterparty risk and with it systemic risk entirely.

claims.claim: If blockchain pushes settlement finality into the seconds range, the entire regulatory infrastructure built to address counterparty and systemic risk would have to be reformed, and most systemic risk and counterparty risk regulation would become unnecessary.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Blockchain-Based Securities Offerings (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3411110
scope_conditions: settlement finality in the seconds range
blockchain based settlement adopted at scale
claims.supporting_quote: Arguably the entire regulatory infrastructure that has been tailored to address counterparty- and systemic risk would need to be reformed if settlement finality can be increased to the seconds range with blockchain technology.

claims.claim: Instant settlement destroys an existing business practice: without the T+3 grace period, institutional investors can no longer lend idle shares to investors covering short positions.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Blockchain-Based Securities Offerings (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3411110
scope_conditions: blockchain based settlement without a grace period
claims.supporting_quote: Without this grace period in a blockchain-based settlement system, institutional investors will no longer be able to lend their idle shares to investors to cover short positions.

claims.claim: The net and compress model used by post trade service providers exists because not every trade must be processed; on some estimates, processing every trade would require an additional 2.9 million orders per day.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Blockchain-Based Securities Offerings (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3411110
scope_conditions: post trade service providers serving large investors
claims.supporting_quote: According to some estimates, if every trade needs to be processed, providers would need to process an additional 2.9 million orders a day.

claims.claim: Neither the Overstock offering nor the Linq based offerings were structured to support widespread ownership or trading through blockchain, and no major exchange or inter-dealer market permits or will foreseeably permit trading of blockchain issued securities.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Blockchain-Based Securities Offerings (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3411110
scope_conditions: U.S. exchanges and inter-dealer markets as of the time of writing
claims.supporting_quote: no major exchange or inter- dealer market permits, or will permit in the foreseeable future, trading of securities issued through blockchain.

claims.claim: A blockchain based offering routed through a single broker produces a specific cluster of risks, including limited price discovery, no market making and therefore less liquidity, constrained short selling, impaired best execution, and no print to a tape or national exchange.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Blockchain-Based Securities Offerings (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3411110
scope_conditions: offering structures with only one authorized broker-dealer
single non-scalable ATS
claims.supporting_quote: Several additional risks are associated with the limited trading and associated limited material liquidity that results from a blockchain-based offering involving only one broker.

claims.claim: Blockchain based offerings introduce technology risks from code design and functioning and from third party intrusions that are generally absent in traditional offerings, and these risks cannot really be quantified.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Blockchain-Based Securities Offerings (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3411110
scope_conditions: blockchain based offerings compared with traditional offerings
claims.supporting_quote: Technology-based risks include risks from the design and functioning of code, and from third-party intrusions. Such risks are generally not present in a traditional offering.

claims.claim: Regulators' relative unsophistication about the technology is itself a risk driver, because a poorly informed regulator is likely to over-react and precipitate new or expanded regulation.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Blockchain-Based Securities Offerings (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3411110
scope_conditions: regulators lacking technical understanding of blockchain
claims.supporting_quote: The relative unsophistication of the regulators and the lack of regulators' understanding of the technology could result in an over-reaction which in turn can precipitate creating new / expanding existing regulations.

claims.claim: Regulatory uncertainty produces a chilling effect: because early adopters must apply traditional law to novel instruments and cannot reach a comfortable level of certainty, legacy businesses hold back from adoption.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Blockchain-Based Securities Offerings (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3411110
scope_conditions: current U.S. regulatory climate for tokens and digital securities
claims.supporting_quote: As a result, there is a chilling effect over the industry where legacy businesses are weary to adopt because of regulatory uncertainty.

claims.claim: Digital securities are not recognized under any state's current commercial law, which matters because that recognition governs margining and the pledging of securities as collateral.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Blockchain-Based Securities Offerings (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3411110
scope_conditions: state commercial law as codified in the UCC
claims.supporting_quote: The lack of recognition of "digital" securities under any state's current commercial law,51 which is relevant for margin / pledging securities as collateral

claims.claim: The regulatory challenges of blockchain based offerings should be addressed by revising federal securities law provisions to recognize digital securities, to permit broad based trading of equity-equivalent digital securities, and to permit their margining.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Blockchain-Based Securities Offerings (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3411110
scope_conditions: U.S. federal securities law
claims.supporting_quote: may be in part addressed by revising several federal securities law provisions to allow: (i) recognition of "digital securities," (ii) broad-based trading of equity-equivalent "digital securities," and (iii) margining of "digital securities."

claims.claim: The SEC has developed neither blockchain-specific offering disclosure standards nor retail investor protection measures particular to blockchain based offerings, leaving issuers without guidance.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Blockchain-Based Securities Offerings (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3411110
scope_conditions: SEC rulemaking and guidance as of the time of writing
claims.supporting_quote: SEC has not identified or developed any blockchain-specific offering disclosure standards, or provided guidance, 2. SEC has not identified or developed any retail investor-protection measures unique / particular to blockchain- based offerings

claims.claim: Near instant settlement creates its own regulatory problem: there is no practical ability to correct trade errors when settlement is same day, whereas the T+2 or T+3 structure supplies a correction window even as its delay causes other trading violations.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Blockchain-Based Securities Offerings (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3411110
scope_conditions: same day or near instant settlement compared with T+2 and T+3
claims.supporting_quote: Settlement-related issues (e.g., no practical ability to correct trade errors because of same-day / near-instant settlement versus T+3 / T+2 structure).

claims.claim: Despite an early call for regulatory leadership from Commissioner Stein in 2015, the SEC has not addressed core recognition questions for blockchain in finance, including cryptocurrencies, tokens as securities, and DAOs as investment advisers.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Blockchain-Based Securities Offerings (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3411110
scope_conditions: SEC action between 2015 and the time of writing
claims.supporting_quote: Despite this early cautioning and call for action, the SEC has not yet addressed core issues pertaining to the recognition of blockchain technology applications in finance.

claims.claim: The SEC's rejection of the Winklevoss Bitcoin ETF, reasoned on Bitcoin's unregulated nature and susceptibility to fraud, reflects agency distrust of the crypto asset class as a whole rather than a narrow product objection.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Blockchain-Based Securities Offerings (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3411110
scope_conditions: SEC order disapproving the Winklevoss Bitcoin Trust listing
claims.supporting_quote: The SEC's decision regarding the Bitcoin ETF reflects its distrust towards the crypto asset class as a whole, especially funds attempting to trade digital currencies.

claims.claim: The SEC's reasoning against the Bitcoin ETF does not transfer to blockchain based private investment funds such as those built on Melonport, because such funds trade a diverse array of cryptocurrencies and reach a much more limited and accredited audience, which curtails investor risk.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Blockchain-Based Securities Offerings (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3411110
scope_conditions: private investment funds limited to accredited investors
funds trading diversified crypto portfolios rather than Bitcoin alone
claims.supporting_quote: Moreover, the audience of a Melonport-type fund is much more limited and curtails the risk to investors.

claims.claim: Delaware's 2017 amendment to the Delaware General Corporation Law recognizing distributed electronic networks or databases as a valid means of creating and maintaining corporate records, including the stock ledger, is the leading state law accommodation of blockchain.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Blockchain-Based Securities Offerings (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3411110
scope_conditions: Delaware corporate law after the 2017 DGCL amendment
records must be convertible into legible paper form
claims.supporting_quote: Most notably, Delaware amended the Delaware General Corporate Law (DGCL) in 2017 to use "distributed electronic networks or databases" to create and maintain corporate records.

claims.claim: Vermont's prudent approach is well founded on its own analysis: the state concluded that at present the costs and challenges of using blockchain for public recordkeeping outweigh the identifiable benefits, while the first mover advantage remains difficult to quantify.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Blockchain-Based Securities Offerings (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3411110
scope_conditions: Vermont public recordkeeping
state report Blockchain Technology: Opportunities and Risk
claims.supporting_quote: at present, the costs and challenges associated with the use of blockchain technology for Vermont's public recordkeeping outweigh the identifiable benefits.

claims.claim: Self regulatory organizations occupy a distinctive position, holding some regulatory authority while remaining beholden to the SEC, which makes them the right actors to educate the SEC toward a more crypto friendly stance by demonstrating successful use cases.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Blockchain-Based Securities Offerings (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3411110
scope_conditions: SROs such as FINRA, Nasdaq, and NYSE that remain subject to SEC oversight
claims.supporting_quote: SROs are also in a unique position to help educate the SEC to becoming more crypto friendly.

claims.claim: Widespread retail investor trading of digital securities, including the ability to margin them, is the linchpin of survivability for blockchain based securities offerings; without retail access the technology may remain marginalized in the offering process.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Blockchain-Based Securities Offerings (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3411110
scope_conditions: retail investor access on a widespread basis
margining of digital securities permitted
claims.supporting_quote: will be the linchpin of survivability and evolution of blockchain-based securities offerings. Without retail investor access, the technology may remain marginalized in the offering process.

claims.claim: Validating blockchain as a cost effective means of supporting securities offerings does not by itself increase capital raising for private companies, because outside of unicorns there is unlikely to be broad retail interest in privately placed digital securities or in securities trading on a single non-scalable ATS.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Blockchain-Based Securities Offerings (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3411110
scope_conditions: privately placed digital securities
securities trading on a single non-scalable ATS
issuers other than unicorns
claims.supporting_quote: Hence, capital-raising opportunities for private companies likely would not be materially increased despite the validation of blockchain technology as a means of cost-effectively supporting securities offerings.

claims.claim: Using blockchain as a more efficient public offering medium will almost certainly require modifying the regulations governing the offering process, the processes for offering, settling, and administering securities, and the roles of market participants built up over decades.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Blockchain-Based Securities Offerings (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3411110
scope_conditions: U.S. public offering infrastructure
claims.supporting_quote: The utilization of blockchain as a more efficient and reliable public offering medium will almost certainly require modifying many of the (i) regulations applicable to the offering process

claims.claim: Governmental endorsement and guidance on crypto investments is essential for future securities offerings involving cryptocurrencies and blockchain, and absent it the gap between the existing regulatory infrastructure and crypto securities investment will inevitably widen as the market grows.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Blockchain-Based Securities Offerings (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3411110
scope_conditions: growth in the market for crypto investments
United States regulatory infrastructure
claims.supporting_quote: As the market for crypto investments grows, the regulatory gap between the existing regulatory infrastructure and crypto securities investment will inevitably increase further.

claims.claim: Development of blockchain based processes will take several years if not decades, so the most likely outcome is that legacy and blockchain based issuance, trading, and settlement systems coexist side by side for the foreseeable future.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Blockchain-Based Securities Offerings (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3411110
scope_conditions: transition period for securities market infrastructure
claims.supporting_quote: will take several years if not decades, and so the most likely circumstance is that legacy and blockchain-based securities issuance, trading, settlement, and related systems and processes will have to co-exist side-by-side for the foreseeable future.

claims.claim: Private blockchains are the rational transitional vehicle for cautious enterprises, because they let firms experiment at relatively low cost and be better positioned when mass adoption occurs, while allowing the corporation to screen access to transaction records.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Blockchain-Based Securities Offerings (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3411110
scope_conditions: corporations apprehensive about the cost and uncertainty of technology upgrades
private permissioned chains with a governance system for access
claims.supporting_quote: By setting companies up on private blockchains, companies can experiment with the technology which allows them to be better positioned when mass adoption occurs while keeping cost relatively low.

claims.claim: The Overstock structure fails to deliver investor privacy, because all existing broker-dealer customer agreements contain provisions allowing the broker-dealer to share the customer's identity, whereas ideally the individual's privacy would be contained.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Blockchain-Based Securities Offerings (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3411110
scope_conditions: existing broker-dealer customer agreements
claims.supporting_quote: For instance, all existing broker-dealer customer agreements included provisions which allows the broker-dealer to share the identity of the customer. Ideally, the privacy of the individual would be contained.

claims.claim: As a foundational technology, blockchain technology builds the infrastructure for decentralized networked governance, which over time creates an environment in which the internal and external monitoring mechanisms previously necessitated by agency problems in corporate governance can be removed.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Solutions for Agency Problems in Corporate Governance (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3373393
scope_conditions: over a multi-decade time horizon
requires the supporting infrastructure components to be built
claims.supporting_quote: As a foundational technology, blockchain technology creates the infrastructure for decentralized networked governance that, over time, creates the environment that enables the removal of internal and external monitoring mechanisms previously necessitated by agency problems in corporate governance.

claims.claim: Blockchain technology produces a substantial increase in the efficiency of the agency relationship and lowers agency costs by orders of magnitude.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Solutions for Agency Problems in Corporate Governance (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3373393
claims.supporting_quote: Blockchain technology facilitates a substantial increase in efficiency in the agency relationship and lowers agency costs in orders of magnitude.

claims.claim: The core agency conflicts that emanate from the separation of ownership by shareholder principals and control by manager agents cannot be fully addressed by the existing theoretical and legal framework, because monitoring agents is inevitably costly and transaction costs abound.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Solutions for Agency Problems in Corporate Governance (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3373393
scope_conditions: under the existing theoretical and legal framework for corporate governance
claims.supporting_quote: However, the core agency conflicts emanating from the separation of ownership (shareholder principal) and control (manager agent) cannot be fully addressed by the existing theoretical and legal framework.

claims.claim: Blockchain is not a disruptive technology but a foundational technology, and its transformational impact therefore takes decades rather than years.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Solutions for Agency Problems in Corporate Governance (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3373393
claims.supporting_quote: blockchain technology is not a disruptive technology, it is a foundational technology whose transformational impact takes decades rather than years

claims.claim: Blockchain use cases involve interdependent structures, so development of any one area alone cannot succeed without the simultaneous existence of multiple additional support structures.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Solutions for Agency Problems in Corporate Governance (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3373393
scope_conditions: applies to complex, interdependent use cases such as corporate governance
claims.supporting_quote: In other words, development of one area alone cannot be successful as the existence of multiple additional support structures are needed.

claims.claim: Applying blockchain to corporate governance requires the relevant authorities, who most likely understand the governance use case but not the technology, to reach consensus on how and when to implement it.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Solutions for Agency Problems in Corporate Governance (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3373393
scope_conditions: corporate governance implementations within existing centralized structures
claims.supporting_quote: in the corporate governance context it requires the authorities, who most likely understand the use case and not the technology, to come to a consensus on how and when to implement such technology for that governance use case.

claims.claim: Agency problems originate from the lack of trust between principals and agents, which itself stems from information asymmetries and agents' opportunistic self-interested behavior.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Solutions for Agency Problems in Corporate Governance (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3373393
claims.supporting_quote: Agency problems originate from the lacking trust between principals and agents.

claims.claim: Because of bounded rationality, incomplete foresight, and information asymmetries, it is impossible for principals to contract for every possible action or inaction of the agent so as to induce the agent to act in the principal's best interests.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Solutions for Agency Problems in Corporate Governance (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3373393
scope_conditions: where principals and agents face bounded rationality and incomplete foresight
claims.supporting_quote: it is impossible for principals to contract for every possible action or inaction of the agent in order to induce the agent to act in the best interests of the principal.

claims.claim: The interests of manager agents and shareholder principals are never fully aligned despite best efforts at monitoring and bonding, so agency losses in the form of residual loss inevitably arise.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Solutions for Agency Problems in Corporate Governance (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3373393
claims.supporting_quote: Despite best efforts at monitoring and bonding, the interest of manager agents and shareholder principals in corporate governance are never fully aligned and agency losses inevitably arise from conflicts of interest between principals and agents, known as residual loss.

claims.claim: Residual loss arises because the cost of enforcing suboptimal contracts between principals and agents always exceeds the benefits of performing the contractual obligations.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Solutions for Agency Problems in Corporate Governance (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3373393
claims.supporting_quote: Residual loss arises because the cost of enforcing suboptimal contracts between principals and agents always exceed the benefits of performing the contractual obligations.

claims.claim: Agency costs are the sum of monitoring costs, bonding costs, and residual loss, and in the corporate context they can be seen as the lost share value resulting from diverging interests between shareholders and corporate managers.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Solutions for Agency Problems in Corporate Governance (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3373393
claims.supporting_quote: As such, agency costs are the sum of monitoring costs, bonding costs, and residual loss.

claims.claim: The standard remedy of appointing outside independent directors to separate decision management from decision control is undermined because CEOs often dominate the board, which makes the separation much more difficult and hurts shareholders.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Solutions for Agency Problems in Corporate Governance (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3373393
scope_conditions: boards where the CEO is dominant
claims.supporting_quote: However, CEOs who often dominate the board make the separation of these functions much more difficult, which hurts shareholders.

claims.claim: Shareholder activism reform by itself has been unable to sufficiently improve the corporate governance system.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Solutions for Agency Problems in Corporate Governance (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3373393
claims.supporting_quote: activism reform by itself has been unable to sufficiently improve the corporate governance system.

claims.claim: Government-sponsored organizational experimentation that enables new business models and new organizational structures is desirable and may be one of the few ways to facilitate the needed corporate governance reform.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Solutions for Agency Problems in Corporate Governance (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3373393
claims.supporting_quote: organizational experimentation that enables new business models and new organizational structures is desirable and valuable and may be one of the few ways to facilitate the much needed corporate governance reform.

claims.claim: The continued popularity of existing corporate governance mechanisms may be a product of path dependencies created by the historical evolution of internal and external monitoring mechanisms, rather than of their effectiveness.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Solutions for Agency Problems in Corporate Governance (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3373393
claims.supporting_quote: The popularity of existing mechanisms to address the agency problems in corporate governance may be related to path dependencies created by the evolution of internal and external monitoring mechanisms in corporate governance

claims.claim: Existing governance mechanisms work well in some firms but are ineffective in others, because agency conflicts and their specific scope differ from firm to firm.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Solutions for Agency Problems in Corporate Governance (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3373393
scope_conditions: across a heterogeneous population of firms
claims.supporting_quote: However, existing governance mechanisms work well in some firms but are ineffective in others.

claims.claim: Supervisory tasks traditionally performed by principals to control their agents can be delegated to decentralized computer networks that are reliable, secure, immutable, and independent of fallible human input and discretionary human goodwill.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Solutions for Agency Problems in Corporate Governance (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3373393
scope_conditions: assumes a functioning decentralized network
claims.supporting_quote: Supervisory tasks that were traditionally performed by principals to control their agents can be delegated to decentralized computer networks that are highly reliable, secure, immutable, and independent of fallible human input and discretionary human goodwill.

claims.claim: Blockchain provides an alternative governance mechanism that eliminates agency costs, meaning the principal's cost of supervising agents, by creating trust in the contractual relationship between principal and agent.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Solutions for Agency Problems in Corporate Governance (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3373393
claims.supporting_quote: Blockchain technology provides an alternative governance mechanism that eliminates agency costs - the principal's cost of supervising agents - by creating trust in the contractual relationship between the principal and the agent.

claims.claim: The immutability of the blockchain and its cryptographic security systems provide transactional guarantees that create trust between principals and agents in the integrity of their contractual relationship, and ensure that no participant can circumvent the rules embedded in blockchain code.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Solutions for Agency Problems in Corporate Governance (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3373393
claims.supporting_quote: The immutability of the blockchain and its cryptographic security systems provide transactional guarantees and create trust between principals and agents in the integrity of their contractual relationship.

claims.claim: A blockchain guarantee means that a contract between principal and agent executes only if and when all contract parameters have been fulfilled by both parties and verified by a majority of miners or nodes in the system.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Solutions for Agency Problems in Corporate Governance (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3373393
claims.supporting_quote: Blockchain guarantees include contract execution between principal and agent only if and when all contract parameters were fulfilled by both parties and verified by a majority of miners/nodes in the system.

claims.claim: Because governance guarantees are embedded in code, there is no need in the blockchain infrastructure for the principal to institute oversight and monitoring, and the associated agency costs disappear.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Solutions for Agency Problems in Corporate Governance (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3373393
scope_conditions: assumes the coded guarantees hold
claims.supporting_quote: Hence, in the blockchain infrastructure, there is no need for the principal to institute oversight and monitoring with the associated agency costs.

claims.claim: It is decentralized network connectivity via the Internet, rather than blockchain's use of digital signatures, that provides the most protection against fraud, because multiple copies of the blockchain are available to all participants across the distributed network.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Solutions for Agency Problems in Corporate Governance (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3373393
scope_conditions: fully distributed, decentralized networks
claims.supporting_quote: blockchain's use of digital signatures helps establish the identity and authenticity of the parties involved in the transaction, it is the completely decentralized network connectivity via the Internet that allows the most protection against fraud.

claims.claim: The distributed consensus model, in which network nodes verify and validate transactions before execution, makes it extremely rare for a fraudulent transaction to be recorded in the blockchain, and it does so without compromising the privacy of the parties.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Solutions for Agency Problems in Corporate Governance (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3373393
claims.supporting_quote: Blockchains' distributed consensus model, e.g. the network "nodes" verify and validate chain transactions before transaction execution, makes it extremely rare for a fraudulent transaction to be recorded in the blockchain.

claims.claim: Cryptographic hashes increase blockchain security and remove the trust barriers in agency relationships that otherwise require monitoring of agents and generate agency costs.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Solutions for Agency Problems in Corporate Governance (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3373393
claims.supporting_quote: Cryptographic hashes used in blockchain technology further increase blockchain security and removes trust barriers in agency relationships that require monitoring of agents and create agency costs.

claims.claim: Smart contracts enabled by blockchain technology allow comprehensive, near error free, and zero transaction and agency cost coordination of agency relationships.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Solutions for Agency Problems in Corporate Governance (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3373393
claims.supporting_quote: Smart contracts enabled by blockchain technology allow for the comprehensive, near error free, and zero transaction/agency cost coordination of agency relationships.

claims.claim: Agency relationships embedded in smart contracts run exactly as coded, without any possibility of opportunistic behavior by the agent, and all contractual terms are public and fully transparent.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Solutions for Agency Problems in Corporate Governance (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3373393
scope_conditions: simple agency relationships; the author later qualifies this for complex relationships
claims.supporting_quote: Agency relationships in smart contracts run exactly as coded without any possibility of opportunistic behavior of the agent. All contractual terms are public and fully transparent.

claims.claim: The removal of checks and balances, agent monitoring, audit requirements, disclosure regimes, market pressure, and executive compensation schemes produces a qualitative shift in efficiency in the agency relationship and in corporate governance overall.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Solutions for Agency Problems in Corporate Governance (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3373393
claims.supporting_quote: The removal of checks and balances in corporate governance, monitoring of agents, audit requirements, disclosure regimes, market pressure, executive agent compensation schemes, among many others, provides a qualitative shift in efficiency in the agency relationship

claims.claim: Decentralized Autonomous Organizations have begun to challenge the core belief that governance necessitates agency, because blockchain enables the removal of agents as intermediaries through code, peer-to-peer connectivity, crowds, and collaboration.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Solutions for Agency Problems in Corporate Governance (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3373393
claims.supporting_quote: Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAOs) have started to challenge the core believe that governance necessitates agency.

claims.claim: The first DAO had no physical address, no jurisdiction able to claim control over it, no directors, managers, or employees, so all the core control mechanisms typically employed by principals in agency relationships were entirely removed.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Solutions for Agency Problems in Corporate Governance (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3373393
scope_conditions: the first DAO, launched May 2016 on Ethereum
claims.supporting_quote: Indeed, it had no directors, managers or employees. In essence, all the core control mechanisms typically employed by principals in agency relationships were entirely removed in the DAO.

claims.claim: Fundamental flaws in the DAO code enabled hackers to transfer one third of total funds to a subsidiary account, and that hack combined with additional technological limitations brought down the first DAO initiative.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Solutions for Agency Problems in Corporate Governance (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3373393
scope_conditions: the first DAO, 2016
claims.supporting_quote: This hack in combination with additional technological limitations brought down the first DAO initiative.

claims.claim: The unifying interest of DAO token holders in raising token value means they will voluntarily perform optimization tasks, because doing so is directly in their own interest.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Solutions for Agency Problems in Corporate Governance (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3373393
scope_conditions: DAO structures where members hold tokens whose value tracks the organization
claims.supporting_quote: the DAO token holders will desire to perform such optimization tasks as it is in their very interest to do so to help increase the value of the DAO tokens.

claims.claim: Once an optimization proponent has made a deal with the DAO, the deal is recorded in the blockchain and the proponent must deliver on the proposal or the contract is cancelled, which enforces performance without a supervisor.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Solutions for Agency Problems in Corporate Governance (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3373393
scope_conditions: DAO proposal and voting structures
claims.supporting_quote: once the optimization proponent has made a deal with the DAO, it's in the blockchain and the proponent is required to deliver on the proposal or her contract is cancelled.

claims.claim: Non-performance reputational penalties in a DAO are entirely free from racial or cultural biases, because the token holders imposing them are unlikely to even know each other.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Solutions for Agency Problems in Corporate Governance (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3373393
scope_conditions: DAOs where token holders are pseudonymous and mutually unknown
claims.supporting_quote: Crucially, non-performance reputational penalties are entirely free from racial or cultural biases and associated implications as the token holders are unlikely to even know each other.

claims.claim: Because the DAO structure functions without supervisors, token holders who conclude they cannot add value on a task can move to more productive endeavors without incurring the penalties that would exist in a traditional hierarchical corporate structure.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Solutions for Agency Problems in Corporate Governance (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3373393
scope_conditions: DAO structures without supervisors
claims.supporting_quote: because the DAO structure functions without supervisors, DAO token holders who decide they cannot add value on a given task can move to more productive endeavors that better utilize their skills without any penalties

claims.claim: Because of the value to effort focus of work flows in the DAO structure, supervision of management and the imposition of legal duties on management are less needed, since there are fewer or no supervisors, so the fiduciary duties on which the traditional regulatory infrastructure relies become less necessary.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Solutions for Agency Problems in Corporate Governance (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3373393
scope_conditions: DAO structures with few or no supervisors
claims.supporting_quote: Because of the value to effort focus of work flows in the DAO structure, supervision of management and imposition of legal duties on management is less needed because there are fewer or no supervisors.

claims.claim: The core issues that afflict centralized governance solutions, including information asymmetries, censorship, opportunism of agents, breaches of fiduciary duties, and fraud, can only be truly removed if and when a truly decentralized public blockchain emerges that is scalable and fully secure.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Solutions for Agency Problems in Corporate Governance (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3373393
scope_conditions: decentralized rather than centralized blockchain implementations
claims.supporting_quote: and fraud or third-party interference, can only be truly removed to fully reform the agency relationship if and when a truly decentralized public blockchain emerges that is scalable and fully secure.

claims.claim: As agency relationships become more complex, a backstop for human behavior becomes necessary, and the claim that smart contract agency relationships run exactly as coded with no possibility of agent opportunism is less likely to hold in complex agency relationships.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Solutions for Agency Problems in Corporate Governance (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3373393
scope_conditions: complex agency relationships
claims.supporting_quote: As agency relationships become more complex, a backstop for human behavior in agency relationships becomes necessary.

claims.claim: Without a decentralized human backstop to code, the immutability of the blockchain and its cryptographic security systems may not be able to create truly transactional guarantees and trust between principals and agents.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Solutions for Agency Problems in Corporate Governance (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3373393
scope_conditions: complex agency relationships
claims.supporting_quote: Similarly, without a decentralized human backstop to code, the immutability of the blockchain and its cryptographic security systems may not be able to create truly transactional guarantees and trust between principals and agents in the integrity of their contractual relationship.

claims.claim: Blockchain-based corporate governance solutions in DAOs require evolutionary blockchain governance protocols, and socially optimal hard-forking rules cannot suffice.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Solutions for Agency Problems in Corporate Governance (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3373393
scope_conditions: DAO-based governance
claims.supporting_quote: Blockchain-based corporate governance solutions in DAOs require evolutionary blockchain governance protocols. Socially optimal hard- forking rules cannot suffice.

claims.claim: The basis of coded blockchain guarantees will itself evolve and require protocol upgrades, and without evolutionary governance upgrades the cost reduction achieved for the agency relationship cannot be maintained.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Solutions for Agency Problems in Corporate Governance (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3373393
claims.supporting_quote: Without evolutionary governance upgrades the cost reduction for the agency relationship cannot be maintained.

claims.claim: Because blockchain is a foundational technology, blockchain-based governance solutions for agency problems depend on the creation of infrastructure components that have not yet been conceptualized in the decentralized technology evolution.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Solutions for Agency Problems in Corporate Governance (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3373393
claims.supporting_quote: blockchain- based governance solutions for agency problems in corporate governance depend on the creation of infrastructure components that have not yet been conceptualized in the decentralized technology

claims.claim: Decentralized systems lack a central intelligence or leadership hierarchy; instead intelligence is distributed through the system and information enters at the edges, closer to where action occurs and where real time information is generated.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization - A Primer on the New Economy (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3406323
scope_conditions: existing decentralized systems
claims.supporting_quote: decentralized systems do not have a central intelligence or leadership system with traditional hierarchies. Instead, the intelligence is spread throughout the system.

claims.claim: Because information flow in decentralized systems is optimized through dynamic feedback effects, such systems mutate and change easily, which makes them more attack resistant and allows them to grow very quickly.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization - A Primer on the New Economy (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3406323
claims.supporting_quote: Decentralized systems can also very easily mutate and change because the information flow is optimized through dynamic feedback effects. As a result, such systems become more attack resistant on multiple levels.

claims.claim: Decentralized commerce is defined as the global exchange of financial instruments, goods, and services via emerging decentralized technologies.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization - A Primer on the New Economy (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3406323
claims.supporting_quote: Decentralized commerce may generically be defined as the global exchange of financial instruments, goods and services via emerging decentralized technologies.

claims.claim: The ICO share of total blockchain startup fundraising collapsed from about 80% to roughly 35% by August 2018, recovered only marginally to 40% to 50% through February 2019, and then fell to 20% in March 2019.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization - A Primer on the New Economy (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3406323
scope_conditions: blockchain startup fundraising, March 2018 through March 2019
claims.supporting_quote: The percentage of ICOs in relation to total fundraising of blockchain startups dropped from 80% to around 35% in August 2018 and only marginally recovered between September 2018 and February 2019 at around 40% to 50% before dropping to 20% in March 2019.

claims.claim: ICOs changed the venture funding market because they provide investors liquidity far faster than the traditional venture capital path to a late IPO or acquisition, letting venture funds capitalize on profits early.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization - A Primer on the New Economy (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3406323
scope_conditions: venture capital funds invested in crypto start-ups
claims.supporting_quote: By contrast, ICOs provide liquidity to investors much faster and allow venture capital funds to capitalize on existing profits early.

claims.claim: During the ICO boom years the venture capital market in the decentralized technology sector ground to a halt, and the later demise of the ICO market reversed the trend back toward venture funding.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization - A Primer on the New Economy (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3406323
scope_conditions: decentralized technology sector during the ICO boom, roughly March 2017 to June 2018
claims.supporting_quote: During the ICO boom years, the venture capital market in the decentralized technology sector ground to a halt.

claims.claim: Decentralized Autonomous Organizations challenge the core belief that governance necessitates agency, because a DAO can operate a governance structure built entirely on software, code, and smart contracts.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization - A Primer on the New Economy (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3406323
scope_conditions: DAOs instantiated on public blockchain platforms such as Ethereum
claims.supporting_quote: Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAOs) have started to challenge the core believe that governance necessitates agency.

claims.claim: Every time decentralization emerges in a given industry, profit margins disappear, as demonstrated by Skype in telecommunications and by Napster and Emule in the music industry.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization - A Primer on the New Economy (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3406323
scope_conditions: industries entered by decentralized systems
historical examples predating decentralized blockchain technology
claims.supporting_quote: Historical evidence has demonstrated that every time decentralization emerges in a given industry, profit margins disappear.

claims.claim: Decentralization transcends the capitalism versus socialism dichotomy because it uses elements of both profit generation and redistribution, organizing economic structures that generate profits while simultaneously redistributing resources.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization - A Primer on the New Economy (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3406323
claims.supporting_quote: Decentralization uses elements of profit generation and redistribution in a way that in effect combines capitalistic and socialistic ideas.

claims.claim: In decentralized systems profit generation rests less on capitalistic economies of scale and more on open source volunteer contributions and greater good perspectives, with profits arising only if and when the solutions become mainstream.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization - A Primer on the New Economy (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3406323
scope_conditions: emerging decentralized solutions for commerce and society
claims.supporting_quote: The profit generation is less based on capitalistic notions of economies of scale but rather revolves around notions of open source volunteer contributions and greater good perspectives for society.

claims.claim: Personal data, preferences, and opinions can only be limitedly commercialized inside centralized structures, whereas in decentralized structures the same assets can be tokenized, valued, and mobilized, including in real time.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization - A Primer on the New Economy (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3406323
claims.supporting_quote: Such assets, e.g. one's data, preferences, opinions etc. currently in centralized structures can only limitedly be commercialized. In decentralized structures such assets can be tokenized, valued, and mobilized.

claims.claim: Decentralized technologies increase consumer and market trust at unprecedented scale, which lowers transaction costs and raises confidence and certainty, thereby facilitating economies of scale that centralized structures may not be able to achieve.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization - A Primer on the New Economy (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3406323
scope_conditions: technology enabled decentralized commerce
claims.supporting_quote: Trust can help lower transaction costs but it also increases consumer and overall market confidence and certainty, which facilitate economies of scale that may not be possible in centralized structures.

claims.claim: Because decentralized cryptocurrency platforms have lower cost structures, they can remove the consumer fees integral to centralized competitors, which eradicates downward pressure on platform worker compensation and creates a more efficient marketplace by removing rent seeking intermediaries.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization - A Primer on the New Economy (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3406323
scope_conditions: decentralized cryptocurrency platforms competing with centralized platforms

claims.claim: Centralized fiat payment systems require consumers to hold an existing banking relationship, while holding and storing cryptocurrencies does not, which gives decentralized payment systems comparative advantages in orders of magnitude.

scope_conditions: payment systems relying entirely on cryptocurrencies
claims.supporting_quote: Centralized fiat payment systems and platforms typically require some form of an existing banking relationship in order for consumers to utilize their services. Holding and storing cryptocurrencies does not require a banking relationship.

claims.claim: The high intermediary fees of centralized fiat payment systems make those systems economically viable only at higher transaction volumes, which creates barriers to entry that decentralized payment systems do not face.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization - A Primer on the New Economy (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3406323
scope_conditions: centralized fiat payment rails intermediated by banks and services such as PayPal
claims.supporting_quote: The fees make it only economically viable for higher volumes of transactions, creating barriers to entry in the process.

claims.claim: Transacting in cash costs United States consumers roughly 200 billion dollars annually, about 637 dollars per person, driven by counting, managing, storing, transporting, guarding, and accounting for bank notes.

scope_conditions: United States
claims.supporting_quote: In the United States, transacting in cash costs the consumer around 200 billion dollars annually - about $637 per person.

claims.claim: The poor and those with less access to institutions bear a disproportionate share of the costs of using cash.

scope_conditions: cash based economies
claims.supporting_quote: Several studies demonstrate that the poor and those with less access to institutions bear a disproportionate share of these costs of using cash.

claims.claim: Growth in stable cryptocurrencies traces back to attempts to combine the benefits of cryptocurrencies and blockchain with remedies for market volatility, and the growth data suggests demand for volatility management products will keep increasing.

scope_conditions: cryptocurrency markets as of 2019
claims.supporting_quote: demand for products that help manage the volatility inherent in other crypto assets is likely to continue to increase.

claims.claim: The low transaction throughput of public blockchains is a core limitation that holds back more advanced distributed applications, which is why decentralized commerce in 2019 remains relegated to cryptocurrency trading and basic smart contracting.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization - A Primer on the New Economy (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3406323
scope_conditions: public blockchains as of 2019
claims.supporting_quote: The low transaction throughputs of public blockchains is a core limitation that holds back more advanced DApps.

claims.claim: Without a core use case other than the store of value provided by Bitcoin, decentralization technology is less likely to proliferate; banking, money transmission, and triple entry accounting are natural but insufficient as universal use cases for public blockchains.

scope_conditions: public blockchains as of 2019
claims.supporting_quote: Without a core use case, other than the store of value (in Bitcoin), decentralization technology is less likely to proliferate.

claims.claim: Mass adoption of decentralized protocols will remain out of reach so long as users must discern and manage public and private keys to wallets, because user access and usability fall short of mass adoption needs.

scope_conditions: existing decentralized technologies as of 2019
claims.supporting_quote: It will be very difficult to educate the public sufficiently to seamlessly adopt decentralized protocols in their daily life if users have to discern and manage public and private keys to wallets, among other concerns.

claims.claim: People will not enter into long term smart contracts without a stable currency to refer to, since no renter and landlord will gamble future wealth on a lease that may halve or double in value in any given month.

scope_conditions: long term smart contracts denominated in volatile cryptocurrencies
claims.supporting_quote: Finally, people will not enter into a long-term smart contract unless they have a stable currency to refer to.

claims.claim: Because cryptocurrencies embody a transferable store of value, the exercise of power over that value inevitably leads back to centralization through economies of scale, creating core points of attack that undermine the very nature of decentralization.

scope_conditions: emergence of a distributed app economy and decentralized commerce
claims.supporting_quote: Because of their disciplining and market stability enhancing effects, stable cryptocurrencies are part of the financial technology infrastructure that will form the backbone of any emergence of the distributed app economy and decentralized commerce.

claims.claim: Smart contracts enable anonymous parties to engage in decentralized commerce because automated contracting self-executes and self-regulates according to mathematical strictures, removing the need for agency and intermediaries almost entirely.

claims.supporting_quote: Most importantly, the smart contract removes centralized guarantors. The smart contract self-regulates. Only limited legal recourse is available if something goes wrong in the execution of the terms of the contract.

claims.claim: Smart contracts fail to accommodate human business interaction because code does not follow the same logic on similar terms as natural human language, so the flexibility in interpreting intent that human dealings require cannot be ensured.

claims.claim: Smart contracts undermine the parties' ability to continue collaborating when unanticipated eventualities arise, because in most cases of unfulfilled parameters the contract will simply cancel out rather than allow partial performance.

claims.claim: The flexibility that human business requires will unlikely ever be attained in existing decentralized protocols unless a decentralized verification system is built into decentralized commerce.

claims.supporting_quote: the needed flexibility in existing decentralized protocols will unlikely ever be attained unless a decentralized verification system is built into decentralized commerce.

the code is law standard is retained

scope_conditions: decentralized systems, as with any prior attempt to organize society
claims.supporting_quote: Without a core common ethical denominator, decentralized systems cannot last, they lose coherence, become attackable, and can be corrupted, leading to suboptimal societal outcomes.

claims.claim: A DAO's profit distribution weights across present workers, past workers, protocol designers, and governance designers should match the DAO's current values, since a greater share for new workers attracts new workers, a greater share for older workers signals long term stability, and a greater share for protocol designers attracts innovation.

claims.supporting_quote: A greater share for new workers will attract new workers, a greater share for the older workers will signal long-term stability, while a greater share for the protocol designers will attract more innovation.

claims.claim: A dynamic, changing set of governance rules can address the problem that any static rule set is gameable, and can establish the incentives necessary to stop such abuses.

claims.claim: Decentralized systems have no central intelligence or hierarchical leadership; intelligence is instead spread throughout the system, and information filters in at the edges where the action is and where most real time information is created.

As one type proliferates, the other types are slowly but increasingly affected, leading to changes that, in turn, affect each other.

claims.claim: A functioning decentralized reputation system requires that counterparties' actions in decentralized commerce endure and become part of a public record: their actions must stick and become part of a meaningful precedence system.

claims.supporting_quote: This necessitates that counterparties' actions in decentralized commerce endure and become part of a public record. In other words, counterparties' actions need to stick. Their actions have to become part of a precedence system that is meaningful.

claims.claim: Insurance underwriting as currently organized imposes significant costs and inefficiencies and erects high barriers to entry, and it provides no democratized access to the underwriting process or collective decision making on risk.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Decentralized Underwriting (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396542
claims.supporting_quote: The insurance market is dominated by a few core players and subject to high barriers to entry for new market entrants. In the current system, democratized access to the underwriting process and collective decision making on risk does not exist.

claims.claim: In the traditional insurance structure, financial distress or bankruptcy of an individual underwriter harms consumers, who lose the protection of their insurance contract and must seek new coverage.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Decentralized Underwriting (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396542
scope_conditions: traditional centralized insurance structure
claims.supporting_quote: Financial distress or bankruptcy of an individual underwriter affects consumers who may no longer be protected by the insurance contract and have to look for new coverage.

claims.claim: The authors propose that insurance underwriting be operated by a Decentralized Autonomous Organization in which cryptocurrency tokens function as claims on the future cash flows of the underwriting business.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Decentralized Underwriting (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396542
claims.supporting_quote: Insurance products can be optimized with emerging decentralized technology. We propose the use of cryptocurrencies as claims on future cash flows of an underwriting business operated by a Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO).

claims.claim: The reputation tokens of the underwriting DAO are separate and distinct from the cash currency that insureds use to pay premia; the two must not be conflated.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Decentralized Underwriting (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396542
claims.supporting_quote: It is important to note that the reputation tokens are separate and distinct from the cash currency that the insured use to pay their premia.

claims.claim: Tokens in the proposed DAO function as reputation because an agent's proportional token holdings will grow over time only if that agent follows sound and successful underwriting practices.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Decentralized Underwriting (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396542
scope_conditions: tokens are minted as rewards for staking on underwritten policies
claims.supporting_quote: We will refer to these tokens on occasion as reputation tokens as an agent's proportional holdings of these tokens is likely to increase over time only if the agent were to follow sound and successful underwriting practices.

claims.claim: Participation in underwriting is gated by token ownership: only token holders may underwrite insurance policies in the DAO, and inbuilt processes assign new business among them.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Decentralized Underwriting (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396542
claims.supporting_quote: First, only token holders are allowed to participate in underwriting insurance policies. Inbuilt processes are used to assign new business to token holders.

claims.claim: Insurance premia are treated as revenue of the entire DAO rather than of the underwriters who wrote the policy, and are shared among DAO participants; consequently the value of a token is a function of the DAO's expected future cash flows.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Decentralized Underwriting (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396542
claims.supporting_quote: Instead, the premia are treated as the revenue of the entire DAO and shared among the DAO participants. Thus, the value of the tokens is a function of the expected future cash flows of the DAO.

claims.claim: Because newly minted reward tokens go only to agents who stake tokens on policies, passive holders are diluted over time, which pushes agents toward active underwriting while still permitting passive investment.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Decentralized Underwriting (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396542
scope_conditions: reward tokens minted per policy underwritten
claims.supporting_quote: Thus, the total number of tokens grows over time. This implies that "passive" agents who hold the tokens purely to receive a share of future premia will find their proportional ownership in the DAO decrease over time.

claims.claim: The design requires underwriters to stake or encumber tokens against each policy they underwrite, and those encumbered tokens serve to secure the underwriters' promises.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Decentralized Underwriting (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396542
claims.supporting_quote: Fourth, the design requires the underwriters to "stake" or "encumber" an appropriate number of tokens against each policy they underwrite. These tokens in effect serve to secure the promises of the underwriters.

claims.claim: The number of tokens an underwriter must encumber is set by a preset formula whose objective is to make the value of the encumbered tokens sufficient to meet any claim arising at any point in the policy's life.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Decentralized Underwriting (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396542
claims.supporting_quote: The number of tokens to be encumbered is based on a preset formula with the objective of ensuring that the value of the encumbered tokens is sufficient to meet any claims that may arise at any point in the life of the policy.

claims.claim: If underwriters decline to reclaim their encumbered tokens, that breach is resolved by selling the encumbered tokens, plus additional freshly minted tokens as needed, in an auction open to current DAO participants and to outsiders wishing to join.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Decentralized Underwriting (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396542
scope_conditions: breach by underwriters on a specific policy
claims.supporting_quote: In such a case, the encumbered tokens, along with additional freshly minted tokens as needed, would be sold in an auction. All current DAO participants as well as outsiders interested in joining the DAO may bid for the tokens in this auction.

claims.claim: A breach by the underwriters of a policy does not amount to a default by the DAO, and under normal market conditions a well designed DAO should experience very few breaches if any.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Decentralized Underwriting (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396542
scope_conditions: normal market conditions
well designed DAO
claims.supporting_quote: Note that a breach by underwriters on a policy does not imply a default by the DAO. Under normal market conditions, a well-designed DAO should experience very few breaches, if any

claims.claim: A breach occurs only when the underwriters concerned believe that the value of their encumbered tokens is less than the payment they would have to make in order to reclaim those tokens.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Decentralized Underwriting (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396542
claims.supporting_quote: Under what circumstances would a breach occur? It would occur only if the underwriters concerned believed that the value of these tokens is less than the payment they need to make in order to reclaim the tokens.

claims.claim: Breach by underwriters will in general happen only after a dramatic shift in the DAO's future prospects, such as a sharp decrease in expected future revenues or a sharp increase in expected payments on outstanding policies.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Decentralized Underwriting (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396542
scope_conditions: dramatic shift in the DAO's future prospects
claims.supporting_quote: In general, this will happen only if there is a dramatic shift in the future prospects of the DAO, such as a sharp decrease in expected future revenues or a sharp increase in expected payments on outstanding policies.

claims.claim: The underwriting use case is broader than traditional insurance: almost any blockchain transaction that does not consist purely of an exchange of digital tokens may require or benefit from underwriting.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Decentralized Underwriting (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396542
scope_conditions: blockchain transactions involving non digital assets or performance
claims.supporting_quote: In fact, almost any transaction on the blockchain that does not involve an exchange of purely digital tokens may require or benefit from underwriting.

claims.claim: Unlike prior token research, the purpose of issuing tokens here is not only to raise capital but also to give owners the opportunity and incentive to develop the DAO's business.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Decentralized Underwriting (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396542
claims.supporting_quote: Another key difference is that in our study, the purpose of issuing tokens is not only to raise capital but also to provide the owners the opportunity and incentive to develop the business of the DAO.

claims.claim: The value of a token is not uniform across tokens: it depends on whether the token is currently encumbered and, for encumbered tokens, the sooner the token is expected to be released from encumbrance the greater its value.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Decentralized Underwriting (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396542
scope_conditions: steady state DAO
claims.supporting_quote: In general, the sooner a token is expected to be released from encumbrance (by the policy on which it is staked terminating due to either a payout or reaching maturity), the greater its value.

claims.claim: The DAO design requires that the value of the tokens staked on a set of policies be large enough to cover the maximum possible liability on those policies, which in turn imposes a minimum condition on the premium charged.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Decentralized Underwriting (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396542
scope_conditions: steady state model with constant M and p
claims.supporting_quote: The design of the DAO requires that v1 should be large enough to cover the maximum possible liability on the M policies against which these tokens are to be encumbered. We will later derive a condition on the premium

claims.claim: Because the total supply of tokens grows at a constant rate each period, the value of individual tokens depreciates over time.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Decentralized Underwriting (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396542
scope_conditions: token supply growing at rate rho per period
claims.supporting_quote: Note that as the total number of tokens is growing at a rate of ρ per period, the value of individual tokens will depreciate over time.

claims.claim: The margin m is stipulated as the premium per dollar in excess of the probability of a claim occurring at some point in the policy's life, and this margin is the quantity that must exceed a derived threshold for the design to hold.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Decentralized Underwriting (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396542
claims.supporting_quote: Thus, m is the amount of premium per dollar in excess of the probability of a claim on the policy sometime during its life.

claims.claim: The DAO is insolvent when the present value of expected cash flows from new policies falls below the expected cash outflow on currently outstanding policies, and in that state the value of a token is negative.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Decentralized Underwriting (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396542
claims.supporting_quote: The DAO will be insolvent if the value of the DAO becomes negative - in other words, if the Present Value (PV) of expected cash flows from new policies is less than the expected cash outflow from currently outstanding (old) policies. If the DAO is insolvent, the value of a token will be negative.

claims.claim: A sufficiently large negative shock to the number of policies issued per period drives the value of the DAO negative and renders the DAO insolvent, so falling new business volume is a principal insolvency channel.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Decentralized Underwriting (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396542
scope_conditions: Mt follows a random walk
one time large decrease in M
claims.supporting_quote: Thus, if ε0 is sufficiently negative and large in magnitude (i.e., if there is a sufficiently large decrease in M), then the value of DAO will become negative and the DAO will become insolvent.

claims.claim: Raising the margin is the available remedy for an insolvency shock, but it is not a clean fix because the effect of a higher margin on future demand must itself be considered.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Decentralized Underwriting (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396542
scope_conditions: insolvency triggered by a negative shock to policy issuance
claims.supporting_quote: Of course, a remedial course of action that could perhaps be taken in period 0 is to increase the margin m if that is possible. However, we would need to consider the impact of an increase in the margin on future demand.

claims.claim: In the DAO structure, provided an adequate token encumbrance system is in place, each agent is individually responsible for the payouts on the policies that agent underwrote, so the burden of holding adequate capital shifts from the entity to each individual agent.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Decentralized Underwriting (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396542
scope_conditions: a good system ensures adequate tokens are encumbered per policy
claims.supporting_quote: each agent is responsible for meeting the payouts on the policies they have underwritten. Consequently, the burden of maintaining adequate capital falls on each individual agent

claims.claim: Aggregate capital under the DAO structure is lower than under a traditional corporate insurer only if the incremental risk that contingent underwriting liabilities add to agents' private portfolios is small enough; the reduction is conditional, not automatic.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Decentralized Underwriting (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396542
scope_conditions: all policies and agents identical
