claims.supporting_quote: By contrast, the reputation- based DevDAO governance design creates a positive-sum game because DevDAO members have incentives to create lasting non- fungible value for the DevDAO by developing a long-term non- fungible record of productive cooperation that in effect improves the DevDAO.

claims.claim: DevDAO member reputation is inflationary by design, so that non use, meaning failure to stake reputation tokens or to vote, causes value depreciation, which incentivizes action and makes liveness faults less likely.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralized Autonomous Organizations – Internal Governance and External Legal Design (2020). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3652481
claims.supporting_quote: The DevDAO member reputation is inflationary in the DevDAO design. As such, non-use, e.g. non-staking of reputation tokens or non-voting, would lead to value depreciation, which incentivizes action and thus value enhancement. Liveness faults become less likely.

claims.claim: Reputation weighted salary distribution defeats sock puppet attacks, because a member who creates ten accounts holding one reputation token each ends up in the same position as one account holding ten reputation tokens.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralized Autonomous Organizations – Internal Governance and External Legal Design (2020). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3652481
scope_conditions: salary is distributed in proportion to reputation token holdings
claims.supporting_quote: This solves the sock- puppet attack because if a DevDAO member creates 10 accounts with 1 reputation token each, it is the same as 1 account with 10 reputation tokens.

claims.claim: Without a legal wrapper, DAOs face potential regulatory enforcement actions and civil liability not only at the organization level but against individual participants.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralized Autonomous Organizations – Internal Governance and External Legal Design (2020). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3652481
scope_conditions: no off chain legal entity has been formed
claims.supporting_quote: Without a legal wrapper, DAOs face potential regulatory enforcement actions and civil liability, not only at the organization level but against individual participants.

claims.claim: Equity funding and token funding are substitutes: because equity investment in a blockchain startup makes issuing a digital currency both less likely and less necessary as a funding source, a market shift back toward equity funding should shrink the total volume of digital currencies issued.

scope_conditions: digital asset and blockchain startups
token issuance treated primarily as a funding mechanism
claims.supporting_quote: Because equity investments in blockchain startups make it less likely and less necessary for the respective startups to issue digital currencies, at least as a funding source, the market for digital currencies and the total volume of issued digital currencies is likely to recede

scope_conditions: digital asset and blockchain startups
2016 to early 2020s
claims.supporting_quote: Since 2016/17, the funding sources for digital asset startups and blockchain startups moved from equity funding to initial coin offerings (ICOs), to equity offerings, and initial exchange offerings (IEOs), just to return back to equity funding in the early 2020s.

claims.claim: The expected growth rate of DeFi, across diverse estimates, is large enough to call into question the long term viability of the existing decentralized technology infrastructure unless core infrastructure improvements are made.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: decentralized finance built on existing public blockchains
growth continues at estimated rates
claims.supporting_quote: Normatively, the paper points out that the expected growth rate of the DeFi, according to diverse sets of estimates, is substantial enough to call into question the long-term viability of the decentralized technology infrastructure without core infrastructure improvements.

claims.claim: The article stipulates a broad definition of digital assets covering all virtual and electronic assets regardless of how regulators name or categorize them, including cryptocurrencies, security tokens, utility tokens, virtual collectibles, stablecoins, and altcoins.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: definition adopted for the purposes of this article
claims.supporting_quote: For the purposes of this article, digital assets are defined broadly. Digital assets cover all types of virtual and electronic assets, regardless of how they are otherwise named or categorized by regulatory agencies, including cryptocurrencies, security tokens,

claims.claim: The assumption by ICO issuers that token sales let them circumvent securities registration and disclosure requirements proved to be a fallacy for many U.S. issuers, who faced increased SEC enforcement actions in late 2019.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: U.S. issuers of tokens in ICOs
post 2017 enforcement environment
claims.supporting_quote: Of course, for many U.S. issuers of tokens in ICOs this presumption became in retrospective a fallacy that should haunt them in the aftermath of increased SEC enforcement actions of ICOs in late 2019.

claims.claim: By 2019 the ICO market had lost its defining advantage over venture capital: because most ICOs between 2018 and 2019 imposed one to three year lockups, neither market offered early liquidity to investors or issuers, making the two substantively similar.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: ICOs conducted between 2018 and 2019
lockup periods of one to three years
claims.supporting_quote: Most ICOs during that period required one to three-year lockup period for their investors. Accordingly, the ICO market in 2019 is very similar to the venture market in the sense that neither of these markets offers early liquidity to investors and issuers.

claims.claim: Once the staggered private sale discounts of up to fifty percent are counted as a cost of capital, the cost structure of an ICO is arguably significantly higher than that of an IPO, notwithstanding the ICO's lower legal and offering expenses.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: ICOs conducted in 2017 and 2018 with staggered discount structures
comparison against average IPO underwriting fees of four to seven percent
claims.supporting_quote: Considering these steep discounts to incentivize earliest possible investments, the cost structure of ICOs is arguably significantly higher than the cost structure of an IPO.

claims.claim: ICO issuance exceeded venture capital financing of startups for the first time in the second quarter of 2017, with $210 million invested through ICOs against $180 million invested through traditional venture capital funds.

blockchain and crypto startups

claims.claim: Initial exchange offerings emerged as a market response to the near disappearance of the ICO market in January 2019, driven by the cryptocurrency exchanges that were most affected by the collapse.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: cryptocurrency exchanges
aftermath of the ICO market collapse in January 2019
claims.supporting_quote: Initial exchange offers ("IEO") 66 evolved as a response to the near disappearance of the ICO market in January 2019.

claims.claim: The IEO reinserts an intermediary into token offerings: the exchange screens the offering and the issuer no longer interacts with investors directly, reversing the direct issuer to investor structure of the ICO.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: initial exchange offerings
token offerings listed on a cryptocurrency exchange
claims.supporting_quote: In an IEO, the cryptocurrency exchange acts as a screening device for token offerings. In an IEO the issuer does no longer interact with investors directly.

claims.claim: Capped ICO raises, adopted by the crypto community to reduce investor uncertainty about platform valuation in uncapped raises, backfire because the cap creates strong incentives for investors to get in first, raising the likelihood of retail investor frenzy.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: capped ICO raises
retail investor participation
claims.supporting_quote: However, capped ICO raises create significant incentives for investors to attempt to get in first, raising the likelihood of retail investor frenzy.

claims.claim: The absence of mandatory disclosure obligations for ICOs leads promoters to make irregular disclosures or none at all as time passes, producing a significant lack of transparency in the ICO market.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: ICO markets without mandatory disclosure rules
post issuance period
claims.supporting_quote: Moreover, the lack of mandatory disclosures for ICOs leads many promoters to make irregular or no disclosures about the platform as time passes, leading to a significant lack of transparency in the ICO market.

claims.claim: ICO sale terms are not fixed at launch: promoters can alter the smart contract to change the sales rules mid course during an offering, a risk factor for retail investors that has no analogue in a registered offering.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: ICOs administered through promoter controlled smart contracts
claims.supporting_quote: Promoters can also alter the smart contract to change ICO sales rules mid-course during an ICO.

claims.claim: Regulatory uncertainty is curtailing the growth of the digital asset industry because investor classes across the spectrum, from retail investors to the largest institutions, are hesitant to participate while the legal treatment of digital assets remains unclear.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: early 2020s digital asset market
absence of sufficient regulatory guidance
claims.supporting_quote: The regulatory uncertainty in the market for digital assets is curtailing the growth of the industry. Many investor classes - from retail to the largest institutions - are hesitant to participate in the market because of the regulatory uncertainty.

claims.claim: Institutional investors face a distinct barrier beyond volatility: fiduciary responsibility to their clients limits the type of risk they may take on, and the lack of custody solutions recognized by regulators compounds the problem.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: institutional investors subject to fiduciary duties
early 2020s absence of regulator recognized custody solutions
claims.supporting_quote: While larger institutional players face the same issues, they are also limited by their fiduciary responsibility to their clients, which limits the type of risk they can be exposed to. Compounding these challenges is the lack of stable custody solution(s) that are recognized by the regulators.

claims.claim: Immature markets such as the market for digital assets in 2020 often cannot attract the institutional investors and venture capitalists who have sufficient operating experience in that market, which is a self reinforcing constraint on market development.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: immature or nascent asset markets
digital asset market as of 2020
claims.supporting_quote: Immature markets, such as the market for digital assets in 2020 often cannot attract institutional investors and venture capitalists that have sufficient operating experience in that market.

claims.claim: Early stage investing in digital assets is a relationships business, and without access to a network of core industry expertise early stage investments in the digital asset industry are rarely successful.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: early stage investors in digital asset startups
claims.supporting_quote: Without access to a network of core expertise early stage investments in the digital asset industry are rarely successful.

claims.claim: Anonymity in decentralized networks imposes a specific design constraint: system architects need a special skillset to navigate the limits that anonymity places on system design, and that skillset remains very rare in the early 2020s.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: decentralized networks with anonymous and autonomous participants
incentive compatible token design
claims.supporting_quote: The anonymity in decentralized networks requires a special skillset for system architects who know how to navigate the limitations in system design that is associated with anonymity.

claims.claim: Because the digital asset market has been so hype driven, technical experience has not added significantly to overall market development and maturity, leaving many top projects in 2020 still afflicted by unresolved technical issues.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: cryptocurrency market through the early 2020s
hype driven market conditions
claims.supporting_quote: Because the market has been so hype driven, technical experience has not added significantly to overall market development and maturity.

claims.claim: Bitcoin functions as a medium of exchange for a number of businesses but arguably fails as a store of value and as a unit of account, because of its volatility and its lack of intrinsic value.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: Bitcoin as evaluated against the three classical money functions
claims.supporting_quote: but it arguably fails as a store of value and as a unit of account because of its volatility and lack of intrinsic value.

claims.claim: Cyber security incidents contribute to the volatility of the digital asset market through a specific channel: consumers instantaneously withdraw their assets from an exchange affected by an incident.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: digital asset exchanges affected by cyber security incidents
author flags other contributing reasons
claims.supporting_quote: Some indicia suggest that cyber security incidents contribute to the volatility of the digital asset market as consumers withdraw instantaneously their assets from an exchange that has been affected by a cyber security incident, among other reasons for this relationship.

claims.claim: Token design must be treated as an iterative process in which data collection and flexibility in core design parameters are essential, because prior crypto economic assumptions routinely turn out to be suboptimal once the network grows and user preferences change.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: token and crypto economic design for growing decentralized networks
claims.supporting_quote: Data collection and flexibility in core design parameters are essential because prior crypto-economic assumptions often materialize as suboptimal in the light of network growth and changing user and consumer preferences.

claims.claim: The evolution of the DeFi market and its new monetary system depends on the stability of DeFi products and digital assets, and both stability and adoption of DeFi are undermined by the instability of most cryptocurrencies.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: DeFi platforms denominated in volatile cryptocurrencies
claims.supporting_quote: The evolution of the DeFi market and its new monetary system depends on the stability of DeFi products and digital assets. Stability and adoption of DeFi is undermined by the instability of most cryptocurrencies.

claims.claim: DeFi platforms grant the unbanked access to the loan market by disintermediating existing banks, connecting borrowers and lenders directly in peer to peer networks and accepting digital assets as collateral with far less documentation than banks require.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: borrowers excluded from centralized banking for lack of documentation
DeFi lending protocols
claims.supporting_quote: DeFi platforms grant the unbanked access to the loan market by disintermediating existing banks. DeFi Dapps connect borrowers and lenders in peer-to-peer networks directly.

claims.claim: The DeFi lending market is highly concentrated: MakerDAO alone accounts for almost ninety percent of the total USD value locked in DeFi projects.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: DeFi projects measured by total USD value locked
period covered by DeFi Pulse data
claims.supporting_quote: MakerDAO accounts for almost ninety percent of total USD value locked in DeFi projects.

claims.claim: Centralized financial technology does not complete the disintermediation it promises, because users still deal with a technology company as intermediary instead of a financial institution, which leaves room for the decentralized solutions DeFi attempts to provide.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: centralized FinTech platforms
peer to peer transaction settings
claims.supporting_quote: In existing centralized forms of financial technology disintermediation users are still dealing with a technology company as intermediary instead of a financial institution.286 Accordingly, centralized financial technology disintermediation is incomplete and allows for further improvements.

claims.claim: DeFi is more efficient than existing financial intermediation including FinTech, and that superior efficiency traces to its extensive reliance on code and automation, which removes large parts of the human element and the errors and inefficiencies that come with it.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: comparison of DeFi with legacy financial intermediation and FinTech
claims.supporting_quote: DeFi is more efficient than existing financial intermediation, including FinTech. Its superior efficiency can be traced to its extensive reliance on code and automation that remove large parts of the human element and the associated errors and inefficiencies.

claims.claim: DeFi's decentralization remains theoretical in one important respect: as of the early 2020s DeFi is still largely relegated to one dominant platform, with 87 percent of all publicly funded DeFi projects built on Ethereum.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: publicly funded DeFi projects
beginning of the 2020s
claims.supporting_quote: At the beginning of the 2020s, DeFi is still largely relegated to the use of one dominant platform. 87% of all publicly funded DeFi projects have been built on Ethereum.

claims.claim: At the beginning of the 2020s DeFi was not sufficiently user friendly, because core interfaces such as metamask, myetherwallet, and scatter require levels of technical know how in handling public and private keys that most lay users do not possess.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: lay retail users of DeFi interfaces
beginning of the 2020s
claims.supporting_quote: At the beginning of the 2020s, DeFi was not sufficiently user friendly.

claims.claim: The digital asset market resulted from a technology push rather than a market pull: developers were driven by technical advancement rather than by usefulness and user friendliness, and market pull may only evolve once the DeFi technology infrastructure is more developed.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: digital asset and DeFi platform development
immature technology infrastructure
claims.supporting_quote: As with most innovative technologies, the digital asset market also resulted from a technology push rather than a market pull.

claims.claim: DeFi platform technologies often have limited product market fit because the reliance on code over human judgment produces products built around automation that ignore the human element in financial transactions.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: DeFi products built primarily on automated code execution
transactions involving subjective or non codifiable inputs
claims.supporting_quote: DeFi platform technologies often have a limited product market fit. The reliance on code in the market for digital assets over human judgments resulted in a focus on products that predominantly rely on automation, ignoring the human element in financial transactions.

claims.claim: Because human interactions in business are often too complex to be fully codified objectively, DeFi systems that exclude all non objective information from their analysis do not fully utilize available information, which limits their efficiency and usefulness.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: DeFi products analyzing only objectively recordable and verifiable inputs
complex commercial interactions
claims.supporting_quote: However, human interaction in business are often too complex to be fully codified objectively. By excluding all non- objective information from the product analysis, all available information may not be fully utilized which limits efficiency and potential usefulness of DeFi

claims.claim: Accountability is a structural concern in DeFi: without a central entity it can become unclear who is responsible for wrongdoing, and when problems arise no central party can freeze transactions, fix problems, or restore normal operations.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: fully decentralized finance systems without a central operator
claims.supporting_quote: "Without central entity involvement, who should be held accountable for potential wrongdoing can become unclear. Who do you resort to for help? When problems arise, no central party can take actions to freeze transactions, fix problems and restore normal operations.

claims.claim: In the early 2020s the DeFi technology infrastructure was insufficiently developed to support DeFi growth estimates and growth potential, and fulfilling that potential requires significant tradeoffs between scaling, security, and levels of decentralization.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: DeFi infrastructure as of the early 2020s
projected DeFi growth rates
claims.supporting_quote: In the early 2020s, the DeFi technology infrastructure was insufficiently developed to support DeFi growth estimates and growth potential.

claims.claim: The tradeoff between transaction approval speed and immutability has the potential to undermine the DeFi infrastructure in the long run.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: consensus based decentralized ledgers supporting DeFi
claims.supporting_quote: The trade-off between transaction approval speed and immutability has the potential to undermine the DeFi infrastructure in the long run.

claims.claim: Consensus in decentralized systems presents a two sided cost problem: creating consensus raises the costs of prepping, processing, and storing information, while reducing the number of computational checks increases the risk of collusion attacks that could change the record.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: public distributed consensus systems
information distributed to and validated by all parties
claims.supporting_quote: Creating consensus requires increase costs of prepping, processing, and storing information.333 On the other hand, fewer computational checks for consensus increase the risk of collusion attacks that could change the record.

claims.claim: Read together with the network capacity failure that CryptoKitties caused on Ethereum in December 2017, the expected DeFi growth rates imply that the Ethereum network will continue to experience network shortages and throughput problems unless its infrastructure is upgraded to handle the expected transaction volume.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: Ethereum network without infrastructure upgrades
DeFi growth continuing at estimated rates
author cautions that correlation is not causation
claims.supporting_quote: the expected growth rate illustrated in Figures [__] and [__] could mean that the Ethereum network will continue to experience network shortages and throughput issues unless the Ethereum infrastructure is upgraded to deal with the expected volume of transactions.

claims.claim: Conducting monetary policy through a central bank digital currency imposes a requirement on the technology layer: the underlying network protocol must enable the central bank to adjust the money supply at will and to act as lender of last resort with access to unlimited supply.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: CBDC built on a blockchain style protocol
central bank intends to conduct monetary policy through the CBDC
claims.supporting_quote: Moreover, in order to be able to conduct monetary policy with CBDC, the underlying network protocol would have to enable the central bank to adjust the money supply at will.

claims.claim: The Bank of Canada's year long Jasper trial revealed a tradeoff rather than a solution: Ethereum would make the wholesale payment system more resilient but was costly and raised privacy issues, while Corda addressed cost and privacy but made the system less resilient, and the Bank concluded in May 2017 that blockchain was not mature enough to run a national interbank payment system.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: Bank of Canada Jasper trial
national interbank payment system use case
as of May 2017
claims.supporting_quote: While Ethereum would make the wholesale payment system more resilient but would be costly and raised privacy issues, Corda was able to address the cost and privacy concerns but made the system less resilient.

claims.claim: Although the public realm of coins could not exist without prior private experimentation, it is possible that the public realm will impact or even pre empt private coin development, for example if central banks attempt to censor the use of digital currencies they did not issue.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: coexistence of central bank digital currencies and privately issued coins
claims.supporting_quote: it is possible that the public realm of the coin evolution could attempt to impact or even pre- empt the private coin development and use. For example, some central banks may attempt to censor the use of non-centrally-issued digital currencies.

claims.claim: The concept of a DAO fails if it becomes centralized, and centralization in governance is the largest single threat to a DAO.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
claims.supporting_quote: The concept of a DAO fails if it becomes centralized. Centralization is omnipresent in computing systems, economics, and society at large. Yet centralization in governance is perhaps the largest threat to a DAO.

claims.claim: Decentralized governance must be dynamic and evolutionary, otherwise the system becomes centralized and brittle over time; most DAOs fail to accomplish this.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: governance that must persist over time
systems relying on information from the edges
claims.supporting_quote: Decentralized governance has to be dynamic and evolutionary in order to avoid for the system to become, over time, centralized and brittle. Most DAOs fail to accomplish this.

claims.claim: Tying a DAO's legal existence to existing legal and jurisdictional frameworks typically requires a representative in the chosen jurisdiction, which centralizes the DAO and results in the failure of the DAO concept.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: DAO anchored in an existing jurisdiction
frameworks that require local representation
claims.supporting_quote: Tying the legal existence of a DAO to any forms of existing legal and jurisdictional frameworks typically results in the need for a representative in the chosen legal framework and jurisdiction, which, in turn, centralizes the DAO and results in the failure of the DAO concept.

claims.claim: Only a jurisdiction that grants a DAO limited liability as an entity and accepts its independent status without requiring representation can be truly favorable to DAO concepts.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: jurisdictions competing to host DAOs
claims.supporting_quote: Only a jurisdiction that gives the DAO limited liability as an entity and accepts its independent status without the need for representation may truly be favorable for DAO concepts.

claims.claim: The focus on value enhancement of fungible tokens can drive short termism in DAOs and cause ethical and governance issues to be ignored.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: DAOs whose incentive design centers on fungible token value
claims.supporting_quote: Yet, the focus on the value enhancement of fungible tokens can lead to short- termism and may ignore ethical and governance issues.

claims.claim: Working with suboptimal layer 1 blockchain solutions that carry high gas fees and low throughput delays the evolution of DAO infrastructure design, because innovation is inhibited by those layer 1 features.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: development anchored to first generation layer 1 networks
claims.supporting_quote: Yet, working with suboptimal layer 1 blockchain solutions with high gas fees and low throughput delay the evolution of DAO infrastructure design as innovation and evolution is inhibited through suboptimal layer 1 features.

claims.claim: Regulatory uncertainty is holding back both the development of DAOs and the potential of DAOs to optimize digital assets.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: regulatory environment of the early 2020s
claims.supporting_quote: Regulatory uncertainty is holding back the development of DAOs and the optimization potential of DAOs for digital assets.

claims.claim: If DAO members do not formalize a legal structure for their entity, courts are very likely to impose one on them, which is a serious risk of DAO membership.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: DAOs with no off-chain legal entity
litigation reaching a court
claims.supporting_quote: However, a very serious risk is associated with DAO membership in the sense that if the DAO members do not formalize a structure for their human-created entity, courts are very likely to impose one for the members of the DAO.

claims.claim: Default general partnership treatment would hold every stakeholder of a DAO liable for any debts or legal actions the DAO faces, exposing known participants to regulatory enforcement and civil actions.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: no legal entity formed
U.S. partnership default rules apply
claims.supporting_quote: Many courts and lawyers would describe the relationship between members of a DAO and their investors as the default general partnership which holds every stakeholder of a DAO liable for any debts or legal actions that the DAO may face.

claims.claim: Private agreements that limit remedies to DAO assets are unlikely to be upheld if the DAO faces a tort suit.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: tort claims rather than contract claims
off-chain dispute settlement
claims.supporting_quote: Parties may be able to limit remedies to DAO assets through private agreements. But, if the DAO should face a tort suit, such an agreement is unlikely to be upheld.

claims.claim: Cybernetic systems change constantly and are less amenable to jurisdictional reach, which makes it nearly impossible to apply a common legal anchor and traditional jurisdictional principles to them.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: constantly changing cybernetic systems
counterparties that do not concurrently exist
claims.supporting_quote: Cybernetic systems are constantly changing and less amenable to jurisdictional reach, making it near impossible to apply a common legal anchor and traditional jurisdictional principles to cybernetic systems.

claims.claim: Under current securities laws, DAOs governed solely by smart contracts are restricted in pooling assets and generating profit, because those laws limit their ability to fund ecosystem development and deploy capital efficiently.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: DAOs governed solely by smart contracts
current U.S. securities law
claims.supporting_quote: Under current laws, DAOs solely governed by smart contracts are restricted in their ability to pool assets and generate profit because securities laws limit their ability to fund ecosystem development and deploy capital efficiently.

claims.claim: Effective institutional governance requires a duality of incentives, namely incentives for actors to improve their own utility while their actions simultaneously benefit the whole institution over the long run, in order to defeat rational and opportunistic attempts to game the design.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: institutions with rational, opportunistic internal and external constituents
claims.supporting_quote: Human nature and any effective machine derivatives of human engagements in institutional form require a duality of incentives in order to overcome attempts of rational and opportunistic internal and external constituents to game the governance design of a given DAO.

claims.claim: When fungible assets are the dominant incentive design in the governance of a DAO with identifiable actors, rational and opportunistic internal and external participants will typically attempt to corrupt that governance design for their own gain.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: fungible assets used as the dominant governance incentive
actors who are identifiable
claims.supporting_quote: When fungible assets are used as the dominant incentive design in the governance of DAOs with identifiable actors, rational and opportunistic internal constituents and external participants will typically attempt to corrupt the governance design of the DAO for their own gain.

claims.claim: The identity of actors in a DAO governance design is itself a source of corruption, so merit identifiers other than individual identity remove the most corruptive influences.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: governance designs that expose actor identity
claims.supporting_quote: Similarly, the identity of actors in a DAO governance design creates typically corruptive elements. Merit identifiers other than individual identity remove the most corruptive influences.

claims.claim: DAOs cannot exist and persist without ever increasing degrees of decentralization, so DAO legal designs must first and foremost supplement the internal decentralization the DAO has achieved.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: long lived DAOs
claims.supporting_quote: DAOs cannot exist and persist without ever increasing degrees of decentralization. Therefore, first and foremost, DAO legal designs need to supplement the internal decentralization accomplished by the DAO.

claims.claim: Existing legal solutions for DAOs typically require some form of legal representation in the relevant jurisdiction, and such representation is always a point of centralization.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: current legal wrappers available to DAOs
claims.supporting_quote: Existing legal solutions for DAOs typically require forms of legal representation in the respective jurisdiction, which are always a point of centralization.

claims.claim: A DAO needs a legal wrapper to represent it, because a DAO cannot by itself rent an office or sign a contract that can only happen on paper.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: DAO operations that touch the real world
claims.supporting_quote: A DAO needs a legal wrapper representing the DAO in the sense that a DAO cannot rent an office or sign a contract that can only happen on paper.

claims.claim: Under the legal wrapper concept individual DAO members are not liable and the third party knows exactly with whom she is interacting and where liabilities arise.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: DAO represented by a legal wrapper entity
claims.supporting_quote: Using the legal wrapper concept, the individual DAO members would not be liable and the third party knows exactly with whom she is interacting and where liabilities arise.

claims.claim: Because a series of smart contracts grants DAO token holders voting rights, those smart contracts take the place of articles of association or bylaws and of the entire precedent system that a jurisdiction based legal structure would otherwise supply by default.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: DAOs running on public decentralized blockchain platforms
claims.supporting_quote: Because a series of smart contracts grants DAO token holders voting rights, the blockchain-based smart contracts imitates the role of articles of association or bylaws and the entirety of a precedent system that would otherwise be provided by default in a jurisdiction-based legal structure.

claims.claim: Governance is the common denominator of the shortcomings in existing DAO infrastructure; it is not a bug or an afterthought in system design but the key feature.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
claims.supporting_quote: The common denominator of the aforementioned shortcomings in the existing DAO infrastructure is governance. Governance is not a bug or an afterthought in system design. Governance is the key feature.

claims.claim: Without continual effort to maintain decentralized order, the values that initially unite DAO members tend to produce ever tighter and more complex hierarchical structures inside the DAO.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: absence of continual decentralization maintenance
claims.supporting_quote: Without continual efforts to maintain decentralized order, values that initially unite DAO members have a tendency to result in ever tighter and complex hierarchical structures in the DAO.

claims.claim: If a DAO's internal voting mechanism is more centralized and carries legacy voting problems, a higher degree of decentralization in its external legal design will typically be canceled out in the long run.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: DAOs pairing centralized internal voting with a decentralized legal design
claims.supporting_quote: if the internal voting mechanism of a DAO is more centralized and afflicted with existing legacy voting issues, a higher degree of decentralization in the external legal design will typically be canceled out in the long run.

claims.claim: The DAO of DAOs uses a duality of internal and external governance: internal governance runs on reputation token staking, while external legal relationships are handled by a legal wrapper that represents the DAO of DAOs in real world legal contexts.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: DAO of DAOs architecture
claims.supporting_quote: For the external legal relationships and governance, the DAO of DAOs is represented in real-world legal contexts by a legal wrapper.

claims.claim: In any open and democratic system, naturally opportunistic rational parties will attempt to circumvent and game the applicable complex static rules to increase their share of power and profit.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: open and democratic systems with complex static rule sets
claims.supporting_quote: In any open and democratic system, naturally opportunistic rational parties will attempt to circumvent and game the sets of applicable complex static rules to increase their share of power and profit within the system.

claims.claim: Because static complex DAO rule sets bring inevitable corruptive gaming and arbitrage behavior, effective DAO governance designs should focus on dynamic elements such as members' ability to re-evaluate existing precedent.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: DAO governance that must both protect members and permit enhancement
claims.supporting_quote: With static complex sets of DAO rules comes inevitable corruptive opportunistic gaming and arbitrage behavior. To avoid these negative effects of static complex DAO rules, effective DAO governance designs should be focused on dynamic elements.

claims.claim: Suboptimal voting outcomes in existing decentralized protocols trace to one token one vote mechanisms, which allocate more power to holders of a significant share of total token supply.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: one token one vote governance designs
claims.supporting_quote: Suboptimal voting outcomes in existing decentralized protocols were associated with the then-popular one-token-one-vote voting mechanisms. A one-token-one-vote design allocates more power to token holders who have a significant share of the total supply of a given token.

claims.claim: Reputation based staking removes the corruptive elements of fungible tokens because third parties are less likely able to take over a non fungible asset such as reputation that is organically grown and maintained through actual expertise in the relevant subject matter.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: reputation staked as a non fungible asset
reputation earned through subject matter expertise
claims.supporting_quote: The corruptive elements of fungible assets/tokens are removed because third parties are less likely able to take over a non-fungible asset, such as reputation, that is organically grown and maintained through actual expertise in a given DAO subject matter.

claims.claim: Reputation voting has two advantages over one token one vote: it is non fungible, which avoids corruptive elements, and it aligns incentives for members individually and for the institution as a whole at the same time.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: DAO of DAOs internal governance
claims.supporting_quote: 1) it is non-fungible which avoids corruptive elements, and 2) it optimally aligns incentives for DAO of DAOs members individually and at the same time aligns their incentives for the totality of the DAO of DAOs as an institution.

claims.claim: In the bifurcated DAO of DAOs token design, non fungible reputation tokens give members voting rights while fungible reputation salary tokens let members earn a salary in proportion to their non fungible reputation holdings.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: DAO of DAOs two token architecture
claims.supporting_quote: 1. the non-fungible reputation tokens give DAO of DAOs members voting rights, and 2. fungible reputation salary tokens allow DAO of DAOs members to earn a fungible salary in proportion to their non-fungible reputation tokens.

claims.claim: Paying members indirectly, through a fungible stable salary proportional to non fungible reputation, removes corruptive elements and makes the governance design more attack resistant and more stable over the long run.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: salary paid in proportion to non fungible reputation scores
claims.supporting_quote: The indirect economic effects remove corruptive elements and make the governance design more attack-resistant and stable in the long run.

claims.claim: Reputation based governance creates a positive sum game because members have incentives to build lasting non fungible value through a long term record of productive cooperation.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: non fungible reputation as the reward
claims.supporting_quote: By contrast, the reputation-based DAO of DAOs governance design creates a positive-sum game because DAO of DAOs members have incentives to create lasting non-fungible value for the DAO of DAOs by developing a long- term non-fungible record of productive cooperation

claims.claim: Member reputation is inflationary by design, so non staking of reputation tokens or non voting leads to value depreciation, which incentivizes action and makes liveness faults less likely.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: reputation that depreciates with non-use
claims.supporting_quote: reputation is inflationary in the DAO of DAOs design. As such, non-use, i.e., non-staking of reputation tokens or non-voting, would lead to value depreciation, which incentivizes action and thus value enhancement. Liveness faults become less likely.

claims.claim: Precedent in the DAO of DAOs is replaced dynamically: if a newer template is referenced more often it becomes the prevailing precedent, while the old precedent dissipates over time through non use.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: decentralized on chain precedent system
claims.supporting_quote: If the new post/template gets more often referenced by the DAO of DAOs members and other users, it becomes over time the new prevailing precedent. The old precedent dissipates over time with non-use.

claims.claim: Charging an admission fee disincentivizes betrayal and defection, because the sunk cost of joining makes cheating expensive when rejoining would also be expensive even under anonymity.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: members who can be blacklisted
anonymous membership
claims.supporting_quote: The DAO of DAOs disincentivizes betrayal and defection by charging an admission fee to become a DAO of DAOs member. Given the sunk cost of joining the DAO of DAOs, it is more expensive for prospective members to cheat because it would be expensive to rejoin even if members could be anonymous.

claims.claim: The opportunity loss from having reputation slashed grows as the network grows, because a larger network means more competition for the reputation tokens that determine fungible salary shares.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: network growth
salary allocated in proportion to reputation
claims.supporting_quote: In the DAO of DAOs design the loss of opportunity from slashing DAO of DAOs member reputation grows as the size of the network increases. In other words, the larger the DAO of DAOs network, the more competition for reputation tokens to receive fungible token salaries.

claims.claim: In the DAO of DAOs, algorithms can exclude cheating members from market access, so punishment becomes automated and therefore credible, and free riding in policing is at least partially eliminated by automation.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: algorithmic contract allocation conditioned on reputation
claims.supporting_quote: By contrast, in the DAO of DAOs, algorithms can be written which exclude DAO of DAOs members who cheat from having access to their market. Punishment for cheating becomes automated and therefore credible. Free riding in policing can at least partially be eliminated by automation.

claims.claim: Superficial identifiers such as language, race, culture, social media profiles, and credit scores play less of a role in DAO of DAOs voting design, which allows inclusion of constituents who have no agency in centralized systems.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: reputation based voting rather than identity based access
claims.supporting_quote: Such relatively superficial identifiers play less of a role in the DAO of DAOs voting designs. The more equal distribution of power in the DAO of DAOs governance design allows the inclusion of constituents who otherwise have no agency in centralized systems.

claims.claim: Reputation weighted salary distribution solves the sockpuppet attack, because a member who creates ten accounts holding one reputation token each ends up in the same position as one account holding ten reputation tokens.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: salary pool distributed in proportion to reputation holdings
claims.supporting_quote: This solves the sockpuppet attack because if a DAO of DAOs member creates 10 accounts with 1 reputation token each, it is the same as 1 account with 10 reputation tokens.

claims.claim: Weighted keys are preferable to NFTs for reputation accounting because the smart contract itself holds the weights and each smart contract may require a different weight for the same key.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: third generation blockchains that provide weighted keys
the same key used across multiple DAO smart contracts
claims.supporting_quote: Weighted keys are preferable to NFTs because the smart contract itself holds the weights and each smart contract may require a different weight for a given key

claims.claim: Any set process or set of rules that can ever be designed will ultimately fail to secure a network for all time, so no static rule set can serve as the permanent foundation of a DAO.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, A Technical Perspective on Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782203
scope_conditions: decentralized networks
open global membership
anonymous participation
claims.supporting_quote: A core precept for the creation of DAOs is the recognition that any set process or set of rules that can ever be designed will ultimately fail to secure a network for all time.

claims.claim: Building effective and efficient DAOs requires three things together: a secure and meaningful reputation system, maximum bureaucratic transparency through a dynamic governance structure, and coherent transcendental values for long-term stability.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, A Technical Perspective on Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782203
scope_conditions: DAOs with open membership to anonymous individuals worldwide
claims.supporting_quote: In this chapter we argue that building effective and efficient DAOs requires a secure and meaningful reputation system, maximum bureaucratic transparency through a dynamic govern- ance structure, and coherent transcendental values for long-term stability.

claims.claim: Strict letter of the law regimes, which the authors call protocol centralization, produce rigid and temporarily efficient hierarchies, but that same rigidity generates instability and eventual collapse.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, A Technical Perspective on Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782203
scope_conditions: historical rule by law systems
rigidly enforced protocols
claims.supporting_quote: When the laws were strict—Rule by Law—then the hierarchy formed rigidly and was very efficient temporarily, before its rigidity led to its instability and eventual collapse. This is pro- tocol centralization.

claims.claim: Protocol centralization, meaning rigid and immediately enforced rules such as those executed by smart contracts, leads to instability unless it is implemented wisely.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, A Technical Perspective on Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782203
scope_conditions: smart contract enforced protocols
politically decentralized networks
claims.supporting_quote: However, protocol centralization leads to instability if it is not implemented wisely.

claims.claim: No static set of rules can perfectly reflect the will of a group without leaving loopholes that adversaries exploit to profit at the majority's expense, and this produces a permanent arms race between policing and those who push the rules to their limit.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, A Technical Perspective on Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782203
scope_conditions: static rule sets
groups containing adversarial members
claims.supporting_quote: No static set of rules can ever perfectly reflect the will of the group without leav- ing loopholes for adversaries to profit at the expense of the majority. There will always be an arms race between policing and those who will push strict rules to the limit.

claims.claim: To achieve stability a DAO must institute a dynamic governance system that includes clear and accessible processes both for amending the rules and for appealing the automated conclusions reached by smart contracts.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, A Technical Perspective on Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782203
scope_conditions: DAOs governed by smart contracts
claims.supporting_quote: Therefore, to achieve stability a DAO must institute a dynamic governance system with a clear and accessible processes for amending the rules and appealing the automated conclusion of smart contracts.

claims.claim: Because decentralized organizations have no leaders and no hierarchy of control, any governance process must be instituted from the very beginning; it cannot be added later by an authority.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, A Technical Perspective on Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782203
scope_conditions: leaderless decentralized organizations
claims.supporting_quote: Since decentralized organizations don't have leaders or a hierarchy of control, any governance process must be instituted from the very beginning.

claims.claim: Impossibility results establish that no static set of rules can eternally sustain a DAO, which is why DAOs must be set up to run with a dynamic set of rules from the very beginning.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, A Technical Perspective on Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782203
scope_conditions: fixed toolsets and fixed rule sets
claims.supporting_quote: The impossibility results show we can never design a static set of rules which will eternally sustain a DAO. But that just means we need to set up DAOs to run from the beginning with a dynamic set of rules.

claims.claim: Condorcet's paradox demonstrates that it is impossible to construct any democratic voting method that will faithfully discover the will of a group, because cyclic preferences can leave no clear winner.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, A Technical Perspective on Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782203
scope_conditions: three or more candidates
any democratic voting system
claims.supporting_quote: Condorcet's paradox5 demonstrates it is impossible to construct any method that will faithfully discover the will of a group, with any type of democratic voting system.

claims.claim: Because a group sometimes genuinely has no consensus to be discovered, network forking is at times inevitable rather than a governance failure that better rules could prevent.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, A Technical Perspective on Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782203
scope_conditions: cyclic or irreconcilable group preferences
decentralized networks whose members can exit
claims.supporting_quote: First, that is a major problem for democracy. Sometimes there is no consensus to be had. This leads to the second conclusion that sometimes network forking is inevitable.

claims.claim: Plurality voting predictably produces a system that swings between two polarized parties who are less acceptable to the majority but strongly preferred by interested minorities, because voters are incentivized to vote for their preferred one of the perceived top two rather than waste their vote.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, A Technical Perspective on Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782203
scope_conditions: plurality voting rules
voters who want their vote to matter
claims.supporting_quote: So plurality voting predictably leads to a system which swings between two polarized parties who are less acceptable to the majority, but strongly preferred by interested minorities—Duverger's Law.

claims.claim: Given a process with static rules and finite, discrete execution, a sufficiently patient and clever minority can always corrupt the process and profit at the majority's expense while following the rules, so no perfect voting system exists.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, A Technical Perspective on Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782203
scope_conditions: static rules
finite discrete execution
three or more options
claims.supporting_quote: A sufficiently patient and clever minority power can always corrupt the process and profit at the expense of the majority, assuming your process has static rules and finite, discrete execution. There is no perfect voting system.

claims.claim: Across all the alternative polling methods explored in the literature, changes both help and hurt: new approaches solve old problems while creating new opportunities for manipulation, a pattern the authors identify with increasing the attack surface.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, A Technical Perspective on Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782203
scope_conditions: alternative voting and polling mechanisms
continuous or weighted voting technologies
claims.supporting_quote: In all the methods dis- cussed the answer has always been that changes both help and hurt. New approaches solve old problems, but they create new opportunities for manipulation.

claims.claim: It is impossible to set up formal rules that keep a group behaving cooperatively in the long run, even if those rules are policed perfectly; the spirit of the law matters more than the letter of the law.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, A Technical Perspective on Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782203
scope_conditions: long run repeated interaction
even under perfect enforcement
claims.supporting_quote: It is impossible to set up formal rules for a group to keep them behaving in a cooper- ative manner in the long run, even if the rules are policed perfectly.

claims.claim: Keeping dynamic rules coherent over the long run requires a decentralized organization to commit to transcendental values as primary, where transcendental means values that cannot be specified precisely, logically, and completely with formal rules.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, A Technical Perspective on Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782203
scope_conditions: decentralized organizations with evolving rule sets
long time horizons
claims.supporting_quote: To keep these dynamic rules coherent in the long run, a decentralized organization must commit to transcendental values as primary.

claims.claim: The efficiency gain from cooperation in repeated games can only be achieved if a policeable reputation system exists: players must have histories and those histories must be available to other players, which makes transparency and communication essential to effective policing.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, A Technical Perspective on Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782203
scope_conditions: repeated games
grim trigger or similar punishment strategies
claims.supporting_quote: This new leap in efficiency as the players cooperate can only be achieved if there is the possibility of creating a policeable reputational system. The players must have a history, and that history must be available to the other players.

claims.claim: However rules are formalized in a realistic setting, there exist strategies that follow the rules yet subvert the intentions of the framers, so legal strategies will always be available that profit an individual adversary at the expense of the group.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, A Technical Perspective on Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782203
scope_conditions: realistic repeated games
players able to precommit to strategies
claims.supporting_quote: This leads to the intuition that however rules are formalized in a realistic situation, there are strategies which follow the rules, but still subvert the intentions of the fram- ers. There are legal strategies that profit the individual adversary at the expense of the group.

claims.claim: Reputation policing games explain why a business will rationally tolerate a small level of theft when policing costs more than the loss, which also explains the rationality of long-term parasitic and bullying relationships and creates a need for careful protocol design to prevent that corruption.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, A Technical Perspective on Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782203
scope_conditions: policing costs exceed the value of the losses
repeated interaction with asymmetric power
claims.supporting_quote: Similar game setups with reputation policing explain the situation where a busi- ness will rationally tolerate a small level of theft when policing is more expensive, such as when a grocer will ignore a street urchin who nabs an apple once per day.

claims.claim: Allowing periodic opportunities for renegotiation lets players escape the grim trigger trap, but it does not improve outcomes overall because it creates new incentives to defect and then gamble on talking one's way out of the punishment.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, A Technical Perspective on Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782203
scope_conditions: repeated games with renegotiation windows
claims.supporting_quote: Or if you allow periodic opportunities for renegotiation, then you might be able to get out of a grim trigger trap. This sounds like it would improve outcomes, but in fact it gives new opportunities for defecting/cheating.

claims.claim: For any game, a new assumption can be added that generalizes the game so that the previous winning strategy becomes a losing strategy and a new winning strategy arises; the authors offer this as a meta-theorem that cannot itself be formalized.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, A Technical Perspective on Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782203
scope_conditions: any formal game model
actors free to change their behavior and desires
claims.supporting_quote: No matter which game you are playing, you can add a new assumption to make a more complicated generalization of the game, so that the previous winning strategy becomes a losing strategy, and a new winning strategy arises.

claims.claim: Any set of rules that can be designed will need amendment as the environment changes, and a network that relies eternally on a static rule set will inevitably become corrupt or irrelevant.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, A Technical Perspective on Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782203
scope_conditions: open global decentralized networks
anonymous membership
changing environments
claims.supporting_quote: Any set of rules that can ever be designed will always need to be amended in the future as the environment changes, to keep the network running healthily. We cannot rely eternally on a static set of rules, or else the system will inevitably become corrupt or irrelevant.

claims.claim: Despite its alluring simplicity, the Code is Law credo taken as an absolute is not an efficient solution for business, because unintended consequences of contracts arise in almost every business arrangement.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, A Technical Perspective on Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782203
scope_conditions: commercial smart contract relationships
unintended consequences of contract execution
claims.supporting_quote: Despite how alluring the simplicity of the Code-is-Law credo is, that extreme pu- ritanical line is not an efficient solution for business.

claims.claim: For mutually beneficial long-term cooperation to thrive, contracts must be reviewable on the assumption of good faith from both parties when unintended consequences arise.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, A Technical Perspective on Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782203
scope_conditions: long-term business cooperation
unforeseeable contract outcomes
claims.supporting_quote: For mutually-beneficial, long-term cooperation to thrive, it is nec- essary to allow review of contracts assuming good faith from both parties when unin- tended consequences arise.

claims.claim: If the decentralized economy is constructed as a zero-sum game, cooperation becomes impossible because the only feasible long-term strategy is maximal extraction, and participants are incentivized to play the most ruthless strategies available against their counterparties.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, A Technical Perspective on Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782203
scope_conditions: zero-sum reward structures
especially where counterparties are anonymous
claims.supporting_quote: a zero-sum game, then cooperation is not possible as the only feasible long-term strat- egy is the pirate code: take anything not nailed down and leave nothing for your op- ponent. Then people are incentivized to play the most ruthless strategies available to hurt the other parties of a contract.

claims.claim: A Code is Law assumption remains necessary for machine-scale commerce, because the multiplicity of options in a dynamically changing market demands instantaneous legal enforcement without waiting for a centralized human response.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, A Technical Perspective on Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782203
scope_conditions: AI enabled IoT devices contracting across supply chains
high frequency automated business interactions
claims.supporting_quote: The multiplicity of options in a dynamically changing market demands instantaneous legal enforce- ment without waiting for a centralized response of human interjection.

claims.claim: Marketing a consensus algorithm as correct by construction is false advertising, because such proofs establish resistance only to the attacks the theorists considered reasonable at the time, not to all possible attacks.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, A Technical Perspective on Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782203
scope_conditions: correct by construction proof of stake designs
adversaries able to invent new attacks
claims.supporting_quote: In the first place, this is simply false advertising. Most people don't understand that CBC doesn't mean it's mathematically proven to be perfectly resistant to all attacks; it's only resistant to the attacks the theorists consider reasonable at the time.

claims.claim: Finding a correct by construction algorithm that incorporates all possible or even all practical assumptions about network status is not possible, because for any set of assumptions about network behavior an actor can break those assumptions by valuing some other result.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, A Technical Perspective on Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782203
scope_conditions: consensus algorithms for open anonymous networks
claims.supporting_quote: Finding a correct by construction algorithm that incorporates all possible, or even practical, assumptions of possible network statuses, is not possible. Given any set of assumptions about how the network will behave, you can always break those assump- tions by valuing some other result.

claims.claim: Since no algorithm can be perfectly secure in all circumstances, protocol developers should redirect effort from proving algorithms correct to building a governance process that updates the algorithm as network circumstances change, rewarding protocol improvement with meaningful reputation instead of leaving attack as the profitable option.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, A Technical Perspective on Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782203
scope_conditions: proof of stake and other consensus protocols
networks facing evolving adversaries
claims.supporting_quote: Given the impossibility of creating an algorithm that will be perfectly secure in all circumstances, we should instead focus on developing a governance process that al- lows us to update our algorithm to adapt to the changing network circumstances to the security level required

claims.claim: The authors hold that the Bitcoin proof of work algorithm is ultimately flawed, that every consensus algorithm is flawed, and that it is not possible to create an algorithm that is not flawed.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, A Technical Perspective on Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782203
scope_conditions: real world networks with changing markets and anonymous actors
claims.supporting_quote: However, we suspect that the Bitcoin PoW algorithm is ultimately flawed. In fact, we believe that every consensus algorithm is flawed. Further we are confident it is not possible to create an algorithm that is not flawed.

claims.claim: Bitcoin's proof of work has produced no protocol violation in more than a decade, meaning no rule breaking message has been incorporated into the finalized blockchain, even though anyone can run a hacked version of the algorithm anonymously at any time.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, A Technical Perspective on Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782203
scope_conditions: Bitcoin proof of work as of 2021
network of millions of users
claims.supporting_quote: Despite the fact that anyone can run any hacked version of the algo- rithm at any time from an anonymous account, there has not been a single protocol violation—meaning no message has been incorporated in the finalized blockchain which breaks the rules of the algorithm.

claims.claim: Charging admission to a DAO disincentivizes defection because the sunk cost of joining makes cheating expensive when rejoining would require paying again, a mechanism the authors identify as costly signaling that works better the more cheaters the surrounding environment contains.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, A Technical Perspective on Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782203
scope_conditions: anonymous membership
environments with many bad actors
claims.supporting_quote: First, we can disincentivize defection/betrayal by charging admission to the DAO. With the sunk cost of joining, it is more expensive to cheat, since then it would be expensive to rejoin even if members could be anonymous. This is described as costly signaling.

claims.claim: Cooperation is sustained only when the promise of future profits outweighs the present value of defecting, so a discount factor that is too low, or a game known to be ending soon, makes defection the rational choice.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, A Technical Perspective on Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782203
scope_conditions: repeated games with end periods
impatient players or high discounting
claims.supporting_quote: Therefore, the promise of future profits must outweigh the present value to en- sure cooperation.

claims.claim: Anonymity increases rather than decreases the value of reputation tokens, because when potential business partners have less knowledge of a counterparty's identity, the number of reputation tokens held becomes the more important signal.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, A Technical Perspective on Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782203
scope_conditions: anonymous or pseudonymous networks
incomplete information about counterparties
claims.supporting_quote: When potential business partners have less knowledge of your identity, the knowledge from the number of reputation tokens you hold becomes more important.

claims.claim: The deterrent power of reputation tokens grows with network size, because the loss of opportunity from having reputation slashed increases as the network gets larger.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, A Technical Perspective on Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782203
scope_conditions: open global networks
digital reputation tokens
claims.supporting_quote: Another advantage to digital tokens in open global networks is that the loss of opportunity from having your reputation slashed grows as the size of the network in- creases.
