claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
claims.supporting_quote: Additionally, none of those criteria reflect how a prospective deal may correlate with one already in the capitalist's investment portfolio.

claims.claim: Significant information asymmetries in venture capital can lead portfolio company managers to engage in opportunistic behavior after an investment is made.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: post investment stage of a VC financing
claims.supporting_quote: Finally, significant information asymmetries can lead managers to engage in opportunistic behavior after an investment is made.

claims.claim: Because venture capitalists typically want to cash out their gains five to ten years after the initial investment, they play an active role in directing portfolio companies toward a merger, acquisition, or public offering, which can carry significant downsides for those companies and their products.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: VC backed portfolio companies approaching the exit window
claims.supporting_quote: because capitalists typically want to cash-out their gains five to ten years after initial investments, they play an active role in directing the company towards a merger, acquisition, or public

claims.claim: Traditional VCs struggle in the digital asset market because of that market's significant volatility and because they lack expertise in a market still dominated by several key specialized players.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: traditional VCs entering digital asset markets
claims.supporting_quote: Among those are the significant volatility of the digital asset market and lacking expertise of traditional VCs in the digital asset market which is still dominated by several key specialized players.

claims.claim: Traditional VCs often cannot effectively compete with the ever increasing array of decentralized token offering avenues.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: digital asset fundraising markets
claims.supporting_quote: Moreover, traditional VCs often cannot effectively compete with the ever-increasing array of decentralized token offering avenues.

claims.claim: Because traditional VCs need to defend their investment choices to their own investors, they are often reluctant to invest in digital asset startups that have little history or sales records.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: traditional VCs accountable to limited partners
claims.supporting_quote: Traditional VCs are often also not able to effectively invest in the digital asset market because they need to defend their investment choices to their own investors. Because of that, traditional VCs are often reluctant to invest in digital asset startups with little history or sales records.

claims.claim: As a rule of thumb in early investment rounds, the lower the information asymmetry the lower the payout, and below a certain threshold of established value venture capitalists will rarely invest at all.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: early investment rounds
claims.supporting_quote: As a rule of thumb in the early investment rounds, the lower the information asymmetry, the lower the payout. Below a certain threshold of established value, VCs will rarely invest.

claims.claim: Alternative early round funding methods matter because they get entrepreneurs over the VC investment threshold or help them bypass the VC model completely.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: technology entrepreneurs below the VC investment threshold
claims.supporting_quote: These alternative funding methods are important to get entrepreneurs over the VC investment threshold, or to help entrepreneurs completely bypass of the VC model.

claims.claim: At its peak in the 2019 cycle the volume of initial coin offerings surpassed venture capital firms and business angels as a fundraising method for startups.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: the 2019 market cycle peak
claims.supporting_quote: At its peak in the 2019 cycle, the volume of ICOs has surpassed VCs and BAs as a fundraising method for startups.

claims.claim: Information asymmetries increase in traditional VC investment rounds because startups are incentivized to self censor when engaging with VCs, having little data to work with and being reluctant to overexpose themselves to prospective investors.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: early round engagement between startups and VCs
claims.supporting_quote: Information asymmetries increase in traditional VC investment rounds as startups are incentivized to self-censor when engaging with VCs, as they have little data to work with, and are reluctant to overexpose themselves to prospective investors.

claims.claim: The typical VC fee based compensation structure can lead to serious shortcomings, including excessive fundraising, suboptimal investments, misevaluation, and overfunding of portfolio companies during a fund's holding period.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: fee based VC compensation arrangements
claims.supporting_quote: The typical VC fee-based compensation structure can lead to serious shortcomings, including excessive fundraising, suboptimal investments, misevaluation, and overfunding of the portfolio companies during a fund's holding period.

claims.claim: Alternative early round funding mechanisms are not necessarily more successful than VCs in early round technology investing, because they tend to act out of intuition and personal experience whereas VCs use a primarily data driven approach to investment decisions and portfolio company evaluation.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: early round technology investing
claims.supporting_quote: Whereas alternative early round funding mechanisms often tend to act out of intuition and personal experience, VC typically use a primarily data driven approach to investment decisions and portfolio company evaluation and supervision.

claims.claim: Alternative early round funding methods frequently fail to provide adequate funding to fully launch a new company, and a significant number of tech startups that rely exclusively on these methods fail.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: startups relying exclusively on alternative early round funding
claims.supporting_quote: these methods frequently fail to provide adequate funding to fully launch a new company. A significant number of tech startups that rely exclusively on these methods fail.

claims.claim: The novelty of reputation as capital lies in the decentralized and democratized capital allocation functionality enabled by the DAO design.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: a VC DAO built on reputation tokens
claims.supporting_quote: The novelty of "Reputation as Capital" lies in the decentralized and democratized capital allocation functionality enabled by the DAO design.

claims.claim: A VC's proportional holdings of reputation tokens are likely to increase over time if the VC follows sound and successful practices by staking reputation tokens on investment proposals and succeeding in the selection of portfolio companies.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: a VC DAO where members stake reputation for or against proposals
claims.supporting_quote: The VC's proportional holdings of these reputation tokens is likely to increase over time if the VC follows sound and successful practices by way of staking the VC's reputation tokens on investment proposals and succeeding in the selection of portfolio companies

claims.claim: Reputation tokens are separate and distinct from the fiat currency or other fungible tokens used to pay for investments in portfolio companies.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: the reputation as capital DAO design
claims.supporting_quote: It is important to note that the reputation tokens are separate and distinct from the fiat currency or other fungible tokens that may be used to pay for investments in portfolio companies.

claims.claim: Only reputation token holders are allowed to participate in the portfolio selection process, which materializes through reputation staking on investment proposals.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: the reputation as capital DAO design
claims.supporting_quote: First and foremost, only reputation token holders are allowed to participate in the portfolio selection process which materializes by way of reputation staking on investment proposals.

claims.claim: Reputation tokens serve as claims on the future cash flows generated by the DAO, with cash flows in fungible cryptocurrencies paid in proportion to each member's non fungible reputation token holding.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: a DAO that distributes returns as reputation salaries
claims.supporting_quote: Second, reputation tokens serve as claims on the future cash flows generated by the DAO. The cashflows in the form of fungible cryptocurrencies are paid in proportion to each DAO members' non-fungible reputation token holding.

claims.claim: The value of the reputation tokens is a function of the return on investment of the DAO.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: a DAO that treats ROI as DAO revenue shared as reputation salary
claims.supporting_quote: Accordingly, the value of the reputation tokens is a function of the ROI of the DAO.

claims.claim: If reputation whales stake reputation on a project and the market commits the capital for that stake, the whales should still receive part of the ROI because it is their reputation that is at stake, and they are not required to commit capital or to support capital calls with liquidity.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: whale reputation that has become meaningful through a track record
claims.supporting_quote: If whales stake but the market commits for their stake with capital, whales should still have the right to receive (part of) the ROI because it is their reputation that is at stake. Whales are not required to commit capital and don't have to support capital calls with liquidity.

claims.claim: Reputation as venture capital must be distinguished from the capital replacement enabled in decentralized underwriting, because in venture capital reputation needs to fill the role of capital for each funded venture deal rather than only when a claim is filed.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: comparison of decentralized underwriting and venture capital DAOs
claims.supporting_quote: reputation in venture capital needs to fill the role of capital for each funded venture deal.

claims.claim: The basic VC DAO model mixes fungible cryptocurrency investment with minted non fungible reputation, and this duality prevents the full benefits that are generated when non fungible reputation is staked alone on deals.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: early phase VC DAO models that combine capital and reputation staking
claims.supporting_quote: Rather, the VC DAO GP invests both fungible cryptocurrency from a pool as well as non-fungible and minted reputation on the portfolio companies. This duality does not allow for the full benefits that are generated if non-fungible reputation is staked alone on the deals.

claims.claim: Because of significant path dependencies in the capital formation and capital allocation processes of existing venture capital models, the ideal typical reputation based capital allocation model is less likely to be created in the short term.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: short term adoption horizon
claims.supporting_quote: because of significant path dependencies in the capital formation and capital allocation process with existing venture capital models, the above illustrated ideal-typical reputation-based capital allocation model in Figure 1 is less likely to be created in the short term.

claims.claim: In the hybrid VC DAO model eighty percent of returns are allocated to investors pro rata as ROI and twenty percent of returns are allocated to the reputation salary pool.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: the hybrid VC DAO model with a traditional legal structure
claims.supporting_quote: 80% of returns are allocated to investors pro rata as ROI. 20% of returns are allocated to the reputation salary pool.

claims.claim: Through the decentralized governance precedent system, projects upvoted by the whale validation pool that have the highest comparative ROI get more citations in the reputation system and continually enhance the reputation of the whale who sourced and proposed them.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: a DAO operating a decentralized governance precedent system
claims.supporting_quote: Through the decentralized governance precedent system, projects that were upvoted by the Whale validation pool and have the highest comparative ROI get more citations in the reputation system and continually enhance the reputation of the whale who sourced and proposed it.

claims.claim: A VC DAO needs a legal wrapper in order to interact with the real world, because otherwise everyone involved in the DAO may be jointly and severally liable in any jurisdiction.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: DAOs transacting with counterparties in the offchain world
claims.supporting_quote: In order to interact with the real world, the VC DAO needs a legal wrapper. Otherwise, everyone involved in the DAO may be jointly and severally liable in any jurisdiction.

claims.claim: The hybrid smart contracting model is defective because VCs are partially incentivized to fund and stake only the best deals while staking on less optimal deals that the market mostly funds, which undermines their long term reputation accumulation.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: models where VCs can stake reputation without proportionate capital commitment
claims.supporting_quote: The problem with this model is that VCs are incentivized partially to fund and stake only on the best deals and stake on the less optimal deals that are mostly funded by the market. This undermines their long-term reputation accumulation

claims.claim: The incentives that undermine long term success of the hybrid model can be mitigated by mandating that staking on deals requires capital commitments, while allowing VCs to lower their capital commitments and increase their staking over time.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: hybrid VC DAO models transitioning away from capital
claims.supporting_quote: It is possible to mitigate these incentives that undermine the long-term success of the system. For example, it is conceivable that staking on deals by VCs mandates capital commitments to the deals but that VCs can over time lower their capital commitments and increase their staking.

claims.claim: A better system emphasizes reputation by prohibiting capital investment into portfolio companies after an initial minting of reputation in proportion to incoming capital.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: the incentive optimized reputation model with smart contracts
claims.supporting_quote: A better system would avoid this scenario by emphasizing the reputation in the system by prohibiting capital investment into portfolio companies after an initial minting of reputation in proportion to incoming capital.

claims.claim: In the non custodial DAO investment club model all of the return on purchase is minted into fungible reputation tokens that get paid as reputation salaries following decentralized governance, which provides the best incentive alignment for members and the highest potential return for all involved.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: the non custodial DAO investment club model with smart contracts
claims.supporting_quote: In this model, all of the ROP is minted into fungible reputation tokens that get paid as reputation salaries following decentralized governance. This model provides the best incentive alignment for DAOIC members with the highest potential return for all involved.

claims.claim: Because the public co purchases alongside DAO investment club members and expects to pay for the right to benefit from the collective wisdom of those members and the deal pipeline they generate, the public should expect to pay the usual two and twenty fees.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: public co purchase alongside a DAO investment club
claims.supporting_quote: Because the public co-purchases with the DAOIC members and expects to pay a price for the right to benefit from the collective wisdom of the DAOIC members and the deal pipeline they can together generate, the public should expect to pay the usual 2/20 fees.

claims.claim: Over time the members of a DAO investment club do not need capital any longer, because the public market funds the deals and members get paid through the twenty percent public return on purchase that is minted into fungible reputation tokens.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: mature phases of a DAO investment club with public co purchase
claims.supporting_quote: Over time, the members of the DAOIC do not need capital any longer. All they need is the ability to stake RNFTs on newly proposed incoming deals. The public market funds the deals and the DAO members get paid via the 20% public ROP minting to fungible reputation token.

claims.claim: Removing capital as a necessity for deal participation creates a very high level of flexibility for DAO investment club members, allowing them to invest without ever being forced to invest, and making capital calls entirely unnecessary.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: DAO investment club phases where the public market funds deals
claims.supporting_quote: The removal of capital as a necessity for deal participation creates a very high level of flexibility for DAOIC members. It allows the DAOIC members to invest if they so choose but it does not force them to invest, under any conditions. Capital calls are entirely unnecessary.

claims.claim: The collective wisdom of DAO investment club members helps hedge against purchase risk, and because decentralized governance with loosely and tightly coupled votes will very likely make all tightly coupled votes unanimous, no member loses reputation NFTs.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: decentralized governance combining loosely and tightly coupled votes
claims.supporting_quote: The collective wisdom of DAOIC members helps hedge against purchase risk. Moreover, because the applicable decentralized governance with loosesly and tightly coupled votes will very likely make all tightly coupled votes unanimous, no DAOIC member loses RNFTs

claims.claim: Reputation as capital has the potential to lower capital requirements for VC businesses significantly and to increase liquidity at unprecedented levels, because VCs can sell their fungible reputation tokens to the market as needed.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: a functioning market for fungible reputation tokens
claims.supporting_quote: Reputation as capital has the potential to lower capital requirements for VC businesses significantly and increase liquidity at unprecedented levels because VCs fungible reputation tokens can be sold to the market as needed by.

claims.claim: The industry is still experimenting with different forms of DeFi capital replacement schemes, and it will take time to filter out those designs that have unanticipated side effects.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: DeFi experimentation that started in 2020
claims.supporting_quote: The industry is still experimenting with different forms of DeFi capital replacement schemes. It will take time to filter out those designs that have unanticipated side effects

claims.claim: Market liquidity depends on trustworthiness, and trustworthiness depends on observed momentum: isolated instances of motion are insufficient, because the observations must be collected into a history before they carry weight and meaning.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: marketplaces seeking liquidity
claims.supporting_quote: To achieve liquidity, marketplaces must be trustworthy. They need momen- tum. It's not enough to achieve motion in any particular instance. Momentum must be observed to give trust to the marketplace. These observations need to be collected in a history to give them weight and meaning.

claims.claim: Governance in a decentralized organization depends on meaningful reputation, and the meaning of any reputation is determined by its history and by how that history is analyzed and presented, which makes historiography a governance variable rather than a neutral record.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: decentralized organizations
claims.supporting_quote: Governance relies on meaningful reputation to de- cide who or what to focus on. The meaning of reputation is determined by its history and how that history is analyzed and presented.

claims.claim: The choice of historiography is a design choice about the architecture of higher order information storage, and because deciding what is true is the judicial function, historiography is effectively the architecture of judicial governance.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
claims.supporting_quote: The choice of historiography is the design choice of the architecture of higher- order information storage. The purpose of the judicial branch is to finalize information storage, to decide what is true. The architecture of history, historiography, is the ar- chitecture for judicial governance.

claims.claim: Any reliance by a DAO on a centralized feature creates a centralized point of failure that threatens the survival of the organization and renders the system technically centralized despite its decentralized appearance.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: DAOs with any centralized dependency, including oracles
claims.supporting_quote: Any time your DAO relies on a centralized feature, that is a centralized point of failure that is a threat to the survival of the organization. That means the system is technically centralized.

claims.claim: Where a DAO is automated around a single centralized point of failure, the work of decentralizing and giving members redundant power is wasted, because the point of failure functions as a supreme leader and full centralization would be more efficient.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: DAO automated around one centralized component
claims.supporting_quote: In that case it would be more efficient to completely centralize around the single point of failure the DAO is automated around. The effort you're making to decentralize and give each member redundant power is wasted, because the point of failure might as well be the supreme leader.

claims.claim: A DAO that relies on a centralized oracle will eventually be exploited, because the people controlling the oracle will become aware of their power over automated contract triggers and, given the competitive nature of capitalism, are right to take advantage of it.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: DAO automated by smart contracts on oracle data
sufficient value at stake
claims.supporting_quote: Eventually, the people who have the relevant power in the centralized oracle will become aware of the power they have over the DAO. Eventually there will be an opportunity to exploit that information.

claims.claim: Legislation is the wrong remedy for oracle exploitation, because the existence of an arbitrage opportunity means systems will evolve around whatever rules exist in order to exploit the advantage; the proper response is to engineer a better system.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: insider information and arbitrage opportunities
claims.supporting_quote: But the very existence of this opportunity for arbitrage means systems will evolve around whatever rules exist to exploit the advantage. Instead of legislating, the proper response is to engineer a better system.

claims.claim: A robust decentralized oracle finds better information because averaging across a crowd is typically better for complex situations, being less subject to the prejudices of individuals who hold more limited information, so overestimates and underestimates offset each other.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: all things being equal
complex situations
claims.supporting_quote: A robust decentralized oracle would find better information. The wisdom of the crowd can be employed to discover the truth. Averaging information is typically better for any complex situation, since they're less subject to the prejudices of the individual, who has more limited information.

claims.claim: Condorcet's Jury Theorem cuts both ways: larger groups of slightly stupid people, defined as being wrong slightly more than half the time, are worse than smaller groups of stupid people, so the idiocy of the mob is the counterbalance to the wisdom of the crowd.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: average member correct less than half the time
claims.supporting_quote: larger groups of slightly stupid people are worse than smaller groups of stupid people. The idiocy of the mob is the counterbalance to the wisdom of the crowd.

claims.claim: An oracle DAO must filter its network so that the average member is correct at least slightly more often than incorrect; once that filter holds, larger and more decentralized networks converge on the truth more quickly and more certainly.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: average member better than chance
no systemic bias
claims.supporting_quote: So an oracle DAO needs to filter its network to guarantee the average member is correct, at least slightly more than they are incorrect. Then the larger and more decentralized the network becomes, the quicker and more certainly it will converge on the truth.

claims.claim: In the SchellingCoin approach to oracle design, members stake reputation tokens on their answer to the question a DApp is asking and are rewarded according to how close they came to the resulting median value, which functions as the game theoretic Schelling point.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: questions with a verifiable focal answer
claims.supporting_quote: The idea is to have your Oracle DAO members stake their reputation tokens on their answer to a question a DApp is asking. Then you reward those closer to the resulting median value

claims.claim: The protocols governing how a particular oracle question is answered should be set by the subject matter experts themselves rather than by a static centralized hierarchy, because the experts know best how their own system can be gamed and how to prevent that gaming to protect their hard earned reputation.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: domain specific oracle questions
claims.supporting_quote: Giving the experts, them- selves, control of their own organization is better than relying on a static centralized hierarchy. The experts know best how to game their own system, and how to prevent gaming to protect their hard-earned reputation.

claims.claim: Robust decentralized oracles do not yet exist despite well funded proposals, because decentralized oracles are themselves DAOs and therefore inherit the same missing incentive structure, governance processes, and history that all DAOs suffer from.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: state of the technology at the time of writing
claims.supporting_quote: Put simply, decentralized oracles are DAOs, so they still lack the proper incentive structure and governance processes and history that all DAOs suffer from.

claims.claim: A decentralized oracle is not secure until it has significant momentum and history, and it is not even truly decentralized until it has a large network of active members.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: oracle networks
claims.supporting_quote: A decen- tralized oracle is not secure until it has significant momentum and history—an oracle is not even truly decentralized until this is achieved, until it has a large network of active members.

claims.claim: Until decentralized oracle protocols are secure and robustly enacted, projects should rely on centralized oracles while keeping the network's monetary value below the level at which the centralized newsfeed would gain an incentive to manipulate the data.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: pre maturity phase of decentralized oracle technology
claims.supporting_quote: Until the decentralized protocol is secure and robustly enacted, it is better to rely on centralized oracles, and make sure your network doesn't grow to gain such a large monetary value that an incentive arises for the centralized newsfeed to manipulate the data.

claims.claim: Oracle DAOs and decentralized finance DAOs face a bootstrapping deadlock because each relies on the other for its very existence, a chicken and egg problem the authors address by having participants prove their worth in a development period before they can charge other DAOs fees.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: early stage decentralized finance ecosystems
claims.supporting_quote: Unfortunately, oracle DAOs and deFi DAOs rely on each other for their very existence. Which will come first, the chicken or the egg?

claims.claim: Centralized civic institutions always become corrupt over time, and that corruption becomes obvious only once a new technology disrupts their operation and reveals their weaknesses.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: centralized civic institutions over long time horizons
claims.supporting_quote: Centralized civic institutions always become corrupt in time. Then this corruption becomes obvious once a new technology disrupts their operation, revealing their weaknesses.

claims.claim: Institutional corruption follows a repeating cycle: people surrender their power of information transmission to institutions that are initially more effective and efficient, those institutions centralize and ossify into corruption, and new technology then allows people to bypass them.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: information transmission institutions
claims.supporting_quote: give up their power of information transmission to centralized institutions which are more effective and efficient. These institutions become corrupt after their hierarchies centralize and ossify, then new technology allows people to by- pass these centrally controlled media institutions.

claims.claim: If transparent democratic institutions are not built to replace the corrupt ones, new opaque centralized institutions will take their place, as Facebook, YouTube, and Twitter already do with secret algorithms that control what stories spread with no democratic oversight.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: current platform era
claims.supporting_quote: If we don't build transparent democratic institutions to replace the corrupt insti- tutions, new opaque centralized institutions will. Already, Facebook, YouTube, and Twitter are creating secret algorithms that control what type of story can be spread through their platforms

claims.claim: Truth discovery in the marketplace of ideas is more effective and efficient when news aggregators are more decentralized: ten newspapers reporting on a story produce a more accurate historical picture than one newspaper reporting on the story ten times.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: marketplace of ideas
competing independent aggregators
claims.supporting_quote: Truth discovery in any market, including the marketplace of ideas, is more effective and efficient when news aggregators are more decentralized. When there are J` newspapers reporting on a story, a more accurate historical picture emerges than when one newspaper reports on the story J` times.

claims.claim: By 2012, ninety percent of the United States media and entertainment industry was controlled by the top six media conglomerations.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: United States media and entertainment industry, 2012
claims.supporting_quote: By X`JX, K`% was controlled by the top L media conglomerations.

claims.claim: American faith in media has fallen in direct correlation with the consolidation of broadcasting power for as long as active statistics have been studied.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: United States
period for which statistics exist
claims.supporting_quote: American faith in media has reliably fallen in direct correlation with the consolidation of broadcasting power, as long as active statistics have been studied.

claims.claim: The most obvious harm from news consolidation is that national and international centralized corporations do not devote the same degree of focus to the interests of the local communities they serve, because love does not scale.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: consolidated national or international news corporations
claims.supporting_quote: The most obvious problem with news consolidation is that national or interna- tional centralized corporations do not devote the same degree of focus to the inter- ests of the local communities they serve.

claims.claim: Contrary to the common fear, wide scale decentralization of media power will not collapse centralized corporations, just as Napster and BitTorrent did not collapse the centralized music companies; decentralization does not take power from centralized actors, it increases everyone's power.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: incumbents willing to participate in the new collaborative networks
claims.supporting_quote: Wide scale decentralization of power in the media will not collapse the power of centralized corporations, any more than file sharing services like Napster and Bit- Torrent6 collapsed the power of the centralized music companies.

claims.claim: Popularity based ranking cannot substitute for editorial control, because people end up relying on unconscious algorithms to determine what is authoritative and the Folk Theorems establish that such algorithms can always be gamed.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: user generated content platforms without editorial control
claims.supporting_quote: People rely on unconscious algorithms which use popularity to determine what is authoritative content. But the lessons of the Folk Theorems again arise, to remind us that such algorithms can always be gamed.

claims.claim: A central authority is perfectly well incentivized to ignore minor problems that only partially eat into its profits, so long as it maintains ultimate control of those profits, which is why platform level abuses persist under centralized ownership.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: platforms with centralized profit control
claims.supporting_quote: A central authority is perfectly well incentivized to ignore minor problems which only partially eat into their profits, as long as they maintain ultimate control of profits.

claims.claim: Existing decentralized news efforts including WikiNews, the Decentralized News Network, and Steemit failed to gain wide adoption because they lacked ambition; the goal should instead be to empower individuals with greater ability to communicate and cooperate.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: decentralized news projects to date
claims.supporting_quote: All of these examples appear to us to have failed to gain wide adoption due to a lack of ambition. The goal should be to empower individuals with greater ability to communi- cate and cooperate.

claims.claim: Reputation in a news DAO must be anchored in fungible currency: new reputation should be minted only when articles connect to profitable endeavors such as advertising, paid analyses, or protocols relied upon for decentralized business contracts.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: news DAOs building meaningful reputation
claims.supporting_quote: articles must have a foun- dational meaning in fungible currency. New reputation should only be minted when the articles are connected to profitable endeavors—advertising, paid analyses, new protocols that are relied upon for decentralized business contracts.

claims.claim: Reviewers in a news review DAO will give honest reviews despite being paid fees, because the reputational system rewards members mostly on the basis of future fees rather than present ones.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: reputation systems weighted toward future fee streams
claims.supporting_quote: Reviewers will be incentivized to give honest reviews despite fees, because the reputational system rewards members mostly based on future fees.

claims.claim: Tracking and aggregating reputations across DAOs can build a more accurate picture of a person's expertise and experiential gaps than traditional educational institutions provide, which would quickly reveal meaningless certification and licensure programs as worthless.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: reputation systems anchored in profitable endeavor
claims.supporting_quote: Tracking and aggregating our reputations in various DAOs can build a more accurate picture of our expertise and experiential gaps than our tra- ditional educational institutions have.

claims.claim: Transparency in a decentralized network is not optional: every function needs to be publicly auditable for people to trust it, because without a central authority to approve code, unexpected malicious behavior can be built into any opaque code.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: decentralized networks without a central approving authority
claims.supporting_quote: Transparency is crucial in a decentralized net- work. Every function needs to be publicly auditable for people to trust it. Without a central authority to approve it, unexpected malicious behavior can be built into any opaque code.

claims.claim: From a game theory perspective the open source culture advocated in the Web3 movement is not sustainable in the long term unless it is married with a culture of respect for history.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: long term horizon
absence of a culture acknowledging past contributions
claims.supporting_quote: the current open source culture advocated in the WebM movement is not sustainable in the long term. Unless we marry it with a culture of respect for history.

claims.claim: The solution to the game theory problem of getting a player to freely give up intellectual property at one stage of a repeated game is to guarantee a reward at a future stage by fostering a culture that acknowledges past contributions, so players seek future fame by distributing their work in the present.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: repeated game with future stages
culture that reliably acknowledges past contributions
claims.supporting_quote: The solution to the game theory conundrum of how to incentivize a player to freely give up their intellectual property at one stage of a repeated game, is by guaranteeing a reward in a future stage, by fostering a culture of acknowledge- ment of past contributions.

claims.claim: A culture of respect for history is unnatural and must be consciously policed, which makes it another of the essential catalyst institutions that has to be deliberately built into the decentralized economy.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: decentralized economies
claims.supporting_quote: It's unnatural to have a culture of respect for history, and needs to be consciously policed—it's another of the essential catalyst institutions which needs to be built into the decentralized economy.

claims.claim: Weighting references so that more value is shared with older posts promotes long term contributions and innovation and increases stability, while less value sharing encourages new contributions and immediate work, so the weighting parameters encode whether the DAO values long term or short term contribution.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: citation graph based reputation systems
claims.supporting_quote: More value-sharing with older posts will promote long-term con- tributions and innovations and increases stability; less value-sharing encourages new contributions and immediate work. How you design the calculation tells us whether you give more value to long-term or short-term contributions.

claims.claim: Reviewing through references enables punishment and reward in DAOs, which shifts members' motivation away from immediate rewards toward the future and encourages delayed gratification and sacrifice for the good of the group.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: DAOs with a functioning citation and review system
claims.supporting_quote: reviewing through references enables punishment and rewards in DAOs which changes the motivations of members from a focus on immediate rewards to the future, encouraging delayed gratification and sacrifice for the good of the group.

claims.claim: Review changes the game theoretical perspective from a single stage game to a repeated game, which produces more efficient cooperation instead of internal competition and is what makes the open source environment sustainable in the long run.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: DAOs where past contributions remain reviewable
claims.supporting_quote: Review changes the game theoretical perspective from a single stage game, to a repeated game. This leads to more efficient cooperation instead of internal compe- tition.

claims.claim: Review creates a decentralized history for a DAO, and that history gives the organization momentum, gives meaning and focus to perception, and is the basis for making governance, understood as steering, more effective.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: DAOs with reviewable histories
claims.supporting_quote: Review helps create a decentralized history for a DAO, which gives them momentum. History gives meaning and focus to our perceptions. History is the basis for making governance (steering) more effective.

claims.claim: Long run stability of a decentralized organization requires the momentum gained from a clear history, but momentum is not sufficient: if the system is not moving toward a healthy and productive goal it will not last long.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: long run survival of decentralized organizations
claims.supporting_quote: To keep a decentralized organization stable in the long run, they need this mo- mentum gained from a clear history. But momentum toward what purpose? If the system is not moving toward a healthy and productive goal, it will not last long.

claims.claim: The most important aspect of a decentralized organization, and the feature that ultimately determines its long term success, is the group's set of transcendental values.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: long term success of decentralized organizations
claims.supporting_quote: The most important aspect of a decentralized organization, the feature that ultimately de- termines its long-term success, is the group's set of transcendental values.

claims.claim: Reputation, not money, is the proper incentive for motivating the most efficient cooperation and long-term stability in business.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: business and commercial organizations
settings where long-term cooperation is the goal
claims.supporting_quote: Reputation is the proper incentive, instead of money, for motivating the most ef- ficient cooperation and long-term stability in business.

claims.claim: Markets collapse when opportunistic behavior saps the efficiency of cooperation: once the environment becomes too adversarial and trust is diminished, collaboration is no longer profitable.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: markets with significant information asymmetries
environments permitting a wide variety of strategies
claims.supporting_quote: when the efficiency of cooperation is sapped by opportunistic behavior. When the environment becomes too adversarial, when trust is diminished, collaboration is no longer profitable. The market collapses.

claims.claim: Strict legal enforcement is an inefficient remedy for opportunism because every unit of energy devoted to policing is energy that could instead have been used to cooperate productively.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
claims.supporting_quote: Strict legal enforcement is not efficient, because all energies devoted to policing are ener- gies that could be used to cooperate productively.

claims.claim: Strict legal enforcement becomes impossible once a market is sufficiently complex and dynamic, because law cannot keep pace with the creative contracts that leading experts continually invent.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: complex and rapidly evolving markets
markets where experts continually improve business arrangements
claims.supporting_quote: Strict legal enforcement is not pos- sible when the market becomes sufficiently complex and dynamic—laws cannot keep up with the creative contracts that arise when leading experts are continually improv- ing business arrangements.

claims.claim: Reputation converts a transaction from a single-stage zero-sum game into a repeated positive-sum game by holding out the promise of future business opportunities, so the value created is the improved reputation of both parties.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: parties expect continued participation in the network
claims.supporting_quote: Reputation does this with the promise of future business opportunities. This changes the transaction from a single-stage zero-sum game into a repeated positive-sum game.

claims.claim: The failure of many DAOs to date is traceable to their reliance on the good will of network members rather than on engineered incentives.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: decentralized autonomous organizations observed to date
claims.supporting_quote: The failure of many DAOs, so far, has been their reliance on the good will of the members of the network.

claims.claim: As a network grows its members become more anonymous and individually less important, which makes cheating more locally enticing and less globally noticeable, so the system eventually collapses once cheating is obviously the best individual strategy.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: networks that grow large
networks lacking a secure reputation mechanism
claims.supporting_quote: As the network grows, however, the members become more anonymous. Individually they become less im- portant, so cheating is more locally enticing and less noticeable globally. Eventually (or immediately) the system will collapse when it becomes obvious cheating is the best individual strategy.

claims.claim: A Web of Trust style reputation ledger, in which each party rates each transaction and reputation is summed with weightings by rater reputation, will have all of its value drained by the sockpuppet attack, because an attacker can build reputation through transactions between their own fake accounts and then use it to cheat.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: open networks that permit account creation
self-reported transaction ratings
claims.supporting_quote: Unfortunately, the sockpuppet attack will suck all value from the network. Setting up fake accounts, an attacker can build their reputation by making transactions be- tween their own accounts. Once their reputation is sufficiently large to trick a mem- ber, they can use it to cheat the system.

claims.claim: Charging transaction fees or imposing KYC identity protocols does not solve the sockpuppet problem: such defenses push the cost of defending the network onto users, and the defense cost equals what it is worth to break the defense while being multiplied across every transaction with every member.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: defenses that tax ordinary transactions
attacker gain from faked reputation exceeds the cost of faking it
claims.supporting_quote: This doesn't help. Such defenses push the cost of defending the network onto the users. The cost to defend it is exactly as much as it is worth to break the defense, except it's multiplied on every transaction with every member in the system.

claims.claim: Reducing member anonymity weakens rather than strengthens a decentralized network, because personal privacy protects members and lets them be more transparent in their dealings without fear of victimization.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: open decentralized networks
claims.supporting_quote: Further, lessening the anonymity of your members weakens the power of the de- centralized network. Personal privacy protects your members, so it's more secure.

claims.claim: The Web of Trust works acceptably for low-value information transmission but should not be used for transactions involving larger wealth in the general economy, which is part of why the scheme it originated in is called pretty good privacy rather than good privacy.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: high value economic transactions
claims.supporting_quote: It works well for low-value infor- mation transmission, but it should not be used for transactions involving larger wealth in the general economy.

claims.claim: The proper solution to reputation security is to give members themselves the power to police their own reputation, because the leading experts in a field are best equipped to invent the regulations for policing their own industry and are best incentivized to defend their own reputation and future profits.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: decentralized networks of domain experts
claims.supporting_quote: The proper solution is to give your members more power over their reputation. Give the members themselves the power to police their own reputation.

claims.claim: Because members of a decentralized network are assumed relatively equal, evidence of all bureaucratic work must be posted in a universally accessible location for eternal review, and every reputation token needs an openly verifiable history just as digital currency creation does without a central verifying authority.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: decentralized organizations without a central verifying authority
claims.supporting_quote: To remain decentralized, all members are assumed to be relatively equal. Therefore, evidence of all bureaucratic work needs to be posted in a universally accessible loca- tion for eternal review.

claims.claim: Reputation must be staked and risked on votes over work evidence, because otherwise the system suffers the Tragedy of the Commons nothing-at-stake problem; staking ensures every expert is motivated to police every reputation-staked action in order to protect the value of their own investment.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: validation pool voting on work evidence
claims.supporting_quote: To avoid the Tragedy of the Commons (the nothing-at- stake problem, "skin in the game"), reputation must be staked and risked with votes on work evidence. This ensures all experts are motivated to police every reputation- staked action, to protect the value of their investment.

claims.claim: Reputation tokens are meaningful only if grounded in something real, so in a profit-seeking DAO all new reputation tokens must be minted in proportion to the fees the DAO earns.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: DAOs devoted to profit
claims.supporting_quote: Whenever a new reputation token is minted, to be meaningful it must be grounded in something real. In any DAO devoted to profit, the foundational object is money. So all reputation tokens need to be tied to the fees the DAO earns.

claims.claim: Newly minted reputation tokens should enter the system neutral, staked half in favor and half against the post that generated the fee, so that existing token holders can judge the action fairly and are not swayed by an unbalanced validation pool created by a large new fee.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: validation pools triggered by fee-generating work
claims.supporting_quote: For security, when a reputation token enters the system, it should be neutral, so that one faction is not favored over another. Validation pools should begin fairly. Newly minted reputation tokens should be staked half in favor, half against.

claims.claim: All fees should be shared with the entire network of reputation holders in proportion to their holdings, because this reputational salary is what makes reputation tokens valuable and future-oriented.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: profit-generating DAOs with reputation tokens
claims.supporting_quote: All fees should be shared with the entire net- work of reputation holders relative to their holdings. This is the key to making reputa- tion tokens valuable and future-oriented.

claims.claim: Distributing salary equitably, for example equally to all members, is self-defeating: the obvious gaming strategy becomes creating multiple accounts and distributing one's work between them, which is why the salary must be reputation-weighted.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: open membership systems where accounts are cheap to create
claims.supporting_quote: If salary is distributed more equitably, say equally to all members, then the obvious strategy for gaming the system is to create multiple accounts and distribute your work between the accounts.

claims.claim: Each new post should be able to reference older posts, so that when a new post is validated it can raise or lower the reputational value of past posts depending on how users come to perceive the precedent.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: forums with permanent post histories
claims.supporting_quote: If the new post is validated, their value can affect the value of past posts positively or negatively. Old posts can have their reputational value change, depending on how important users perceive the precedent for the system.

claims.claim: Reputation tokens must have their power limited to their proper domain: for each different expertise there must be a separate type of non-interchangeable reputation token, so that a token carries power only within the DAO whose members hold that specific skill.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: organizations spanning multiple domains of expertise
claims.supporting_quote: Reputation tokens need to have power limited to their proper domain, meaning that for each different expertise, there is a separate type of non-interchangeable reputa- tion token.

claims.claim: DAOs are free to organize as they choose, and those that fail to find the right incentives for productive behavior will certainly go extinct, because the feedback loop that includes customers outside the DAO punishes unproductive DAOs by loss of fees.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: DAOs that depend on outside customer fees
competitive markets for DAO services
claims.supporting_quote: DAOs have the freedom to organize any way they choose. If they fail to find the right incentives for productive behavior, they will cer- tainly go extinct. The feedback loop that includes customers outside the DAO naturally punishes any unproductive DAOs, by loss of fees.

claims.claim: Because eternally perfect protocols are impossible, as illustrated by Arrow's Impossibility Theorem and the Folk Theorems of Game Theory, the remedy is not a better static ruleset but a system that continually improves its protocols and smart contracts in reaction to market change.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: governance systems that must adapt over time
claims.supporting_quote: The impossibility of creating eternally perfect protocols, as illustrated by Arrow's Impossibility Theorem and the Folk Theorems of Game Theory, is addressed by a sys- tem which continually improves protocols and smart contracts to react to changes in the market.

claims.claim: Reputation dilates time: it slows immediate transfers of wealth so that past and future enter present decisions, with future-oriented incentives supplied by reputation-based salaries and past-oriented incentives supplied by the editability of reputation.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: systems where reputation can be retroactively slashed or augmented
claims.supporting_quote: Reputation dilates time. It allows us to slow down immediate transfers of wealth, allowing us to consider the future and the past. Future-oriented incentives come from reputation-based salaries. Past-oriented incentives come from the editability of repu- tation.

claims.claim: In hierarchical structures where members are siloed and have few formal connections across tiers, letting service providers create the regulations produces moral hazard, because the provider has an incentive to weaken standards and regulations.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: hierarchical, siloed organizations
self-regulation by service providers
claims.supporting_quote: In a hierarchical structure, where members are siloed and have few formal connections with those immediately above and below their tier in the hierarchy, this leads to the moral hazard problem that the service pro- vider has an incentive to weaken the standards and regulations.

claims.claim: Sockpuppet attacks are inevitable in any organization that wants open membership and anonymous members, and since those properties are essential to the autonomy that makes a global decentralized organization efficient, reputation must be weighted every time it is used.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: open membership
anonymous or pseudonymous members
claims.supporting_quote: Sockpuppet attacks are inevitable if you want the membership to be open and to allow anonymous members. These properties are essential for fostering the individual autonomy that makes a global decentralized organization efficient and powerful.

claims.claim: Every single reputational implementation the authors have audited in the blockchain DAO space carries the flaw of vulnerability to the sockpuppet attack on the Web of Trust model.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: blockchain DAO reputation systems audited by the authors as of writing
claims.supporting_quote: This is the flaw in every single reputational implementation we've audited in the blockchain DAO

claims.claim: SingularityNet's reputation system, which tracks self-reported transaction quality, transaction value, duration of satisfaction, and prior reputation weights, will have its value eroded by the sockpuppet attack once the system becomes valuable enough to merit attack, because it does not implement the other necessities.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: systems implementing only a subset of the seven necessities
once the reputation becomes valuable enough to merit attack
claims.supporting_quote: Without implementing the other necessities, the sockpuppet attack will eventually erode their value, once it becomes valuable enough to merit the attack.

claims.claim: With the balanced staking and fee-sharing necessities implemented, the cost of faking reputation is at an absolute minimum double the value of that reputation, which is how reputation is made more valuable than money.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: both the balanced staking necessity and the shared salary necessity are implemented
claims.supporting_quote: With #e and #j implemented, the cost of faking your reputation is (at an absolute minimum) double the value of the reputation.

claims.claim: Concentration of power is the greatest threat to any decentralized organization, because a single member or sub-coalition that gains a majority of power in an inherently democratic organization will eventually control it no matter what safeguards are in place, at which point the organization is no longer decentralized.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: democratic decentralized organizations
especially profit-devoted and therefore competitive ones
claims.supporting_quote: The idea is that if a single member, or even a sub-coalition, gains j\% of the power in an inherently dem- ocratic organization, they will eventually control it, no matter what the safeguards are.

claims.claim: Fair accounting and transparency in reputation promote decentralization, because customers who can reliably compare reputation harness the available talent rather than waiting for the most talented provider to become free, which keeps reputation differences from accumulating.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: customers can observe and compare member reputations
claims.supporting_quote: Fair accounting and transparency in reputation promotes decentralization. When customers can reliably compare reputation, they are able to harness the available tal- ent, instead of waiting for the most talented to become available.

claims.claim: A reputation token is inherently worth more to the person who earned it than to someone who merely bought it, because of its secondary use in making future earnings, so reputation is harder to accumulate than cash and economies of scale are weakened.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: non-fungible reputation tokens with individual slashable histories
claims.supporting_quote: A reputation token is inherently more valuable for a person who deserves it, than for someone who merely bought it, because of its secondary use in making future earnings.

claims.claim: Because reputation tokens are constantly created, the reputation economy is inflationary, and a member with very high reputation must do proportionally more work merely to maintain the disparity, which makes reputation less likely to concentrate and acts as a natural counterbalance to accumulation of individual power.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: steady state growth, not exponential growth of customers
members of comparable talent
claims.supporting_quote: If one member happens to have a very high reputation, they need to do proportionally more work to maintain the disparity, making reputation less likely to concentrate when people have comparable talent.

claims.claim: One-person-one-vote governance fails on technical questions because half the members have less than average expertise yet equal power, which incentivizes experts to gain power by catering to less expert prejudices instead of pursuing the most effective decisions.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: organizations voting on matters requiring expertise
claims.supporting_quote: Under a one-person-one-vote system, half of the mem- bers have less than average expertise, but equal power. This incentivizes experts to gain power by catering to less expert prejudices instead of following the most effective decisions.

claims.claim: Contemporary blockchains cannot support the proposed architecture because the technology is too slow and expensive to poll members on every transaction, and the messages required for all nodes to register all votes on every action multiply into an unmanageable number.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: blockchains as of writing, including Ethereum
polling on every member action
claims.supporting_quote: Voting is not efficient on contemporary blockchains.

claims.claim: Reputation-based governance faces a chicken and egg problem: voting becomes more efficient once reputation is valuable, but reputation cannot become valuable without meaningful voting.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: bootstrapping a reputation system on existing infrastructure
claims.supporting_quote: This is another chicken and egg problem. Voting will be more efficient with valu- able reputation. Reputation can't be valuable without meaningful voting.

claims.claim: A meaningful reputational system with the potential for retrospective review would let a network rely on fewer nodes, since randomly selected nodes staking their reputation can do the polling work and be reviewed and punished later, which is one reason proof of stake is more efficient than proof of work.

anonymous counterparties
code-is-law smart contract execution
claims.supporting_quote: Self-executing, self-regulating smart contracts between anonymous parties in an open system, create a near perfect zero- sum situation—unless your DAO also includes reputation.

claims.claim: Giving all people more power produces a liquid meritocracy in which leaders are continually rediscovered immediately where and when they are needed, and secure meaningful reputation gives that meritocracy momentum and history.
